# Book text: 100 Old-House Fixes That Save You Thousands

- **Channel:** Roger the Pipe Guy. **Author:** Roger the Pipe Guy (as printed on the cover and title page; written in his own voice).
- **Exact printed title** (used in CTA markers): 100 Old-House Fixes That Save You Thousands. The title page adds the subtitle "Roger the Pipe Guy’s No-Nonsense Guide to Plumbing, Leaks, Drains, Fixtures, Water Damage, Seasonal Maintenance, and Costly Repairs You Can Prevent Yourself". ("Visual Upgrade" in the PDF's file name is not printed in the book.)
- **What's in it:** six parts, 16 chapters and 100 numbered fixes, plus front matter (safety disclaimer, "No Guarantee of Savings or Results", how to use the book, introduction, callout legend, contents) and back matter (100-fix master checklist, emergency shutoff sheet, seasonal calendar, symptom-to-first-check guide, contractor-call preparation sheet, tools and cheap parts list, glossary, resources, about Roger). Every fix has the same six labelled parts: "The Problem", "Why It Costs Money", "Roger’s First Check", "Cheap Fix", "Call a Pro" and "Money Saved". Each chapter opens with an introduction and a "Roger’s Rule" and closes with a "Before You Move On" paragraph; each part has an opener page and a "Part N Recap". After most chapters come one or two full-page illustrations (26 in all), such as maps, flowcharts and labelled photos. The callout legend (page 7) also lists "Old-House Clue", "Do Not Ignore" and "Tools Needed", but no fix uses those labels.
- **Source:** the PDF in the channel's ebook folder on Google Drive (100_Old_House_Fixes_That_Save_You_Thousands_Visual_Upgrade.pdf, 124 pages), converted to text on 2026-10-21. The PDF itself isn't stored here. This is the channel's current book; the older "Rogers_Ultimate_Plumbing_Playbook" PDF on Drive is a different book and isn't covered here.
- **Page numbers:** the book prints its page numbers at the bottom of each page, and they match a PDF reader's page count exactly (PDF page 63 is printed page 63). The cover and the 26 full-page illustrations print no number. Each marker below shows the printed number when there is one. **A CTA cites the printed page number**, because that's what the viewer sees on the page; don't cite an unnumbered illustration page.
- **Conversion note:** the text pages have a real text layer, so they were extracted directly, not by OCR. Words the typesetter split at a line end are joined again (for example "replace-ment" is given as "replacement"); real hyphens are kept. Tables are rebuilt as Markdown tables, and bold and italics are dropped. The cover and the 26 full-page illustrations are pictures: their words were read by OCR and checked by eye against the page images. In those transcriptions, the bracketed notes and the "Photo labels:" and "Diagram labels:" groupings were added during conversion, a colon joins each room or season to its items, and the repeating footer line in each image is left out. Pictures without words aren't described.
- **Use:** for checking which pages cover a video's topic and which facts a CTA may state about the book. It supplies no facts, steps or numbers to the script itself.

Important Safety Disclaimer
Old houses can be unpredictable. Behind a wall, under a sink, beneath a floor, or
inside a basement ceiling, there may be aging pipes, hidden shutoff valves,
deteriorated fittings, unsafe electrical conditions, mold, asbestos-containing
materials, lead paint, structural damage, gas lines, or other hazards that are not
visible until work begins.
The information in this book is provided for general educational purposes only. It
is not a substitute for professional inspection, licensed plumbing work, code-compliant repair, engineering advice, environmental testing, or emergency service.
Always follow local building codes, permit requirements, manufacturer instructions,
and the recommendations of qualified professionals in your area.
If a repair involves gas lines, sewer backups, electrical wiring, structural damage,
active flooding, contaminated water, lead service lines, asbestos, mold, major
water-heater work, or anything you are not fully comfortable handling, stop and
call a qualified professional. Saving money is smart. Taking unnecessary risks is
not.
Roger’s Rule: If you do not know where the shutoff is, do not start taking
things apart.

## Page 3 (printed page 3)

No Guarantee of Savings or Results
This book explains practical checks, preventive steps, and repair-awareness
strategies that may help homeowners avoid unnecessary service calls, spot small
problems before they become large ones, and ask better questions when hiring
contractors. However, every home is different. Actual repair costs, savings, risks,
code requirements, and outcomes depend on the condition of the house, the skill
level of the person performing the work, the materials used, and local labor rates.

Nothing in this book guarantees a specific dollar amount of savings, repair
outcome, or home-value improvement. Use your judgment, work safely, and bring
in a licensed professional when a problem is beyond basic homeowner maintenance.

| Situation | Recommended Action |
|---|---|
| You smell gas or suspect a gas leak | Leave the area and call emergency services or the gas utility immediately. |
| Water is actively flooding the home | Shut off the water if safe, protect electrical hazards, and call for urgent help. |
| Sewage is backing up into fixtures | Stop using water and contact a qualified drain or plumbing professional. |
| A repair requires opening walls or floors | Check for electrical, structural, moisture, pest, lead, and asbestos risks first. |
| You feel unsure about the repair | Stop and call a professional before the problem becomes more expensive. |

How to Use This Book
This book is built for the owner of an older house who wants to make smarter
repair decisions before money starts flying out the door. You do not need to read it
like a textbook. You can read it straight through if you want a full education, but
the real value is in using it as a practical field guide: open to the problem area,
read the fix, check the warning signs, and decide whether this is something you
can safely handle or something that needs a professional.

Old houses usually do not fail all at once. They give clues first. A slow drain, a
sweating pipe, a soft spot near a toilet, a mystery smell in the basement, a water
heater making new noises, or a fixture that suddenly loses pressure can all be early

## Page 4 (printed page 4)

warnings. The goal of this book is to help you catch those clues before they turn
into a ruined ceiling, a flooded basement, a mold problem, or a service call that
could have been avoided.

Roger’s Rule: The cheapest repair is usually the one you catch early.

Each of the 100 fixes follows a simple pattern. First, you will learn what the issue
is and why it matters in an older home. Then you will see what to check, what
tools or supplies may be involved, what mistakes to avoid, and when it is time to
stop and call a qualified professional. The point is not to turn every homeowner
into a plumber or contractor. The point is to help you stop guessing.

| Section Element | What It Helps You Do |
|---|---|
| The Fix | Understand the practical action or inspection step. |
| Why It Saves Money | See how a small check can prevent a larger repair bill. |
| Old-House Warning Signs | Spot clues that are easy to miss in aging homes. |
| DIY Confidence Level | Decide whether this is basic homeowner maintenance or a professional job. |
| Roger’s Rule | Remember the blunt, practical takeaway before you act. |

Before you try any repair, locate the relevant shutoff valve, clear the work area,
take photos before disassembly, and do not force old parts. In older houses, the
part you touch is sometimes stronger than the pipe, fitting, tile, plaster, or framing
around it. A five-minute job can become expensive when an old valve snaps, a
brittle drain fitting cracks, or a hidden leak gets worse.

Use this book in three ways. First, use it as a prevention checklist by walking
through the chapters season by season. Second, use it as a problem-solving guide
when something looks, sounds, or smells wrong. Third, use it as a contractor
conversation tool so you can ask better questions, understand what is urgent, and
recognize when a quote does or does not make sense.

If you remember only one thing, remember this: saving money on an old house
does not mean doing everything yourself. It means knowing what to check, what to
maintain, what to document, what to ignore, and what not to touch. That judgment
is what keeps old-house ownership from turning into one surprise bill after another.

## Page 5 (printed page 5)

Introduction: Old Houses Do Not Have to Drain
Your Wallet
If you own an old house, you already know the deal. The place has character,
history, better bones than a lot of new construction, and at least one repair waiting
around the corner to surprise you. Maybe it is a slow drain that keeps coming
back. Maybe it is a toilet that rocks a little more than it should. Maybe it is a
mystery stain on the ceiling, a shutoff valve that looks like it has not moved since
the last century, or a basement pipe you have been meaning to ask somebody
about.
Here is the truth: old houses are not automatically money pits. They become
money pits when small clues get ignored, simple maintenance gets skipped, and
homeowners do not know what they are looking at until the damage is already expensive.
That is why this book exists.
100 Old-House Fixes That Save You Thousands is not written to make you fearless. Fearless gets people in trouble. This book is written to make you sharper. The
goal is to help you notice problems earlier, understand what is normal and what is
not, and avoid paying for avoidable damage. Sometimes that means doing a basic
fix yourself. Sometimes it means shutting the water off, taking a few photos, and
calling the right professional before things get worse.
Roger’s Rule: A smart homeowner does not guess. A smart homeowner
checks.

Old houses have their own language. They creak, drip, sweat, smell, stain, settle,
clog, and complain in little ways long before they hand you a big bill. Once you
learn how to read those signs, you can protect your home without turning every
weekend into a repair emergency.
This guide focuses heavily on plumbing because plumbing problems are some of
the fastest ways an old house can become expensive. A cracked supply line,
hidden toilet leak, failing water heater, bad drain slope, dripping shutoff, or slow
ceiling leak can cause more damage than most people expect. But the book also
covers related old-house issues that homeowners run into around bathrooms,
kitchens, basements, laundry areas, exterior drainage, seasonal maintenance, and
contractor conversations.

| What This Book Helps You Avoid | Why It Matters |
|---|---|
| Unnecessary service calls | You learn what to check before picking up the phone. |
| Small leaks becoming major damage | Early clues can prevent ruined floors, ceilings, and cabinets. |

This book does not tell you to do dangerous work. It does not tell you to ignore
code. It does not tell you to gamble with gas, sewage, electrical hazards, structural
damage, or contaminated materials. What it does is give you a practical way to
think before you spend: check the simple things, understand the warning signs,
know your limits, and act before the problem becomes a bigger one.

Owning an old house rewards the people who pay attention. You do not need to
know everything. You just need to know enough to stop the obvious mistakes,
catch the early warnings, and avoid getting surprised by problems that were trying
to announce themselves all along.

So before you call a contractor, before you tear something apart, before you
assume the worst, start here. Walk the house. Check the shutoffs. Look under the
sinks. Listen to the drains. Watch for stains. Learn what your home is telling you.

That is where the savings begin.

Callout Legend
The book uses the same handful of field-manual labels again and again so you can
skim fast without missing the point. When you see Roger’s First Check, start there
before you buy a part. When you see Cheap Fix, you are looking at a low-cost
habit, adjustment, cleaning step, or part that may save a service call. When you see
Old-House Clue, slow down and pay attention because the house is giving you an
early warning.

## Page 10 (printed page 10)

Chapter 1 — The Old-House
Emergency Map
If you own an old house, you already know one thing for sure: surprises come
standard equipment. A drip behind the wall, a leak under the sink, or a burst pipe
in the basement can turn from a minor annoyance into a wallet-emptying disaster
before you know it. That’s why the first fixes in this book aren’t flashy upgrades
or fancy tools—they’re about control. Control over water, control over damage,
and control over your time and money.
Fixes 1 through 6 in this chapter are your emergency map. They’re the stuff you
handle before you call a plumber, before you buy a replacement valve, and definitely before you turn off your water and flood the floor. Knowing where your
shutoffs are, testing them without breaking anything, labeling everything, and
making a simple emergency plan for your family can save you hundreds or even
thousands down the road. And building a small emergency kit for quick fixes
means you’re prepared when time and water are against you.
Some repairs are best left to pros—especially in old houses where a wrong move
can mean busted pipes or bigger leaks. So this chapter also tells you the six jobs
you should never try yourself. Save your sweat for the fixes that actually save
money.
Roger’s Rule: Know your shutoffs and how to use them before you need
them. It’s the simplest way to stop a small leak from becoming a house-wide
flood.

Fix 1 — Find Your Main Water Shutoff Before You Need It
The Problem: When a pipe bursts, every second counts. If you don’t know where
your main water shutoff is, water keeps flowing, soaking floors, walls, and
belongings. In old houses, shutoffs aren’t always where you expect them—sometimes buried behind drywall or down in cold, dark basements.
Why It Costs Money: Delayed shutoff means more water damage and bigger repairs. Water running unchecked can ruin drywall, wood floors, and even electrical
systems.

## Page 11 (printed page 11)

Roger’s First Check: Hunt down your main water valve and make sure you
can get to it fast. Check the basement, crawlspaces, near the water meter, or
even outside in a covered box.
Cheap Fix: Mark the location with a piece of tape or a permanent marker on
the wall.
Call a Pro: If you can’t find it or the valve is stuck rusty, have a plumber
locate and replace it with a ball valve that’s easier to use.
Money Saved: Avoid one emergency call and water damage repair—$500 to
$2,500.

Fix 2 — Test the Main Shutoff Without Breaking It
The Problem: Old valves get rusty and stiff. When the time comes, they might
break or refuse to close fully.
Why It Costs Money: A broken valve can mean a bigger leak or needing an expensive emergency plumber to replace it immediately.
Roger’s First Check: Turn the valve slowly once or twice a year to keep it
from seizing up. Don’t force it—if it doesn’t move, stop.
Cheap Fix: Spray some penetrating oil on the valve stem and wait. Then try
again carefully.
Call a Pro: If the valve won’t move or leaks when shut, have a plumber
replace it with a modern ball valve.
Money Saved: Avoid emergency valve replacement and water damage—
$600 to $1,500.

Fix 3 — Label Every Fixture Shutoff in the House
The Problem: Under sinks, behind toilets, and near appliances, shutoffs are often
hidden or unlabeled. In an emergency, hunting them down wastes precious time.
Why It Costs Money: When you can’t shut off the right valve fast, you risk
flooding and costly repairs.

## Page 12 (printed page 12)

Roger’s First Check: Identify every shutoff valve inside your house, then
use waterproof labels or colored tape to mark what they control.
Cheap Fix: Use inexpensive waterproof tape and a permanent marker.
Call a Pro: If valves are missing or corroded, have a plumber install new
shutoffs at each fixture.
Money Saved: One fast shutoff can prevent damage of $75 to $250.

Fix 4 — Make a One-Page Emergency Map for Your Family
The Problem: In a crisis, everyone panics. Family members may not know where
to go or what to do.
Why It Costs Money: Hesitation or confusion can mean bigger leaks, more
damage, or a late call to the plumber.
Roger’s First Check: Draw a simple floor plan showing every shutoff valve
and how to get to them. Keep it near your main electrical panel or front door.
Cheap Fix: Use plain paper and a pen—no fancy tools needed. Make sure
everyone in the house knows where it is.
Call a Pro: If you want a professional home inspection that includes plumbing shutoff map, some plumbers offer this service.
Money Saved: One quick family response can avoid emergency repairs
worth hundreds.

Fix 5 — Build a $50 Leak Emergency Kit
The Problem: When a leak starts, a slow drip can turn into a rushing flood before
you get help.
Why It Costs Money: Without quick fix tools, small leaks can cause expensive
water damage.
Roger’s First Check: Put together a kit with pipe repair tape, rubber
patches, a pair of pliers, a bucket, and a flashlight. Keep it near your main
shutoff.
Cheap Fix: Buy materials from your local hardware store.
Call a Pro: Use your kit only for temporary fixes. Call a plumber ASAP for
permanent repairs.
Money Saved: Stop leaks early to save $150 to $600.

## Page 13 (printed page 13)

Fix 6 — Know the Six Jobs You Should Not DIY
The Problem: Old houses are tricky. Some plumbing repairs can turn into disasters
if you’re not a pro.
Why It Costs Money: A botched repair can cause bigger leaks, code violations, or
safety hazards.
Roger’s First Check: Don’t tackle gas line repairs, main sewer line replacement, water heater installations, cast-iron drain removal, lead pipe
replacement, or electrical-wet-area plumbing yourself.
Cheap Fix: Learn to recognize these jobs and budget to call a licensed
plumber.
Call a Pro: Always hire licensed pros for these six jobs.

draw a simple map your family can use in a hurry. Put together a small emergency
kit so you’re not scrambling for tape or tools when water’s running where it
shouldn’t. These simple, upfront steps won’t fix your plumbing, but they’ll save
you money by keeping small problems small. Take the time now—your future
self will thank you when a leak shows up at midnight.

Fix 7 — Use the Flashlight Test Under Every Sink
The Problem: Old pipes and fittings under sinks hide leaks that start as tiny drips
or condensation. These often go unnoticed until you’ve got water damage or mold
behind the cabinet.
Why It Costs Money: If you miss early signs, that slow drip can rot wood, ruin
flooring, or feed mold behind walls—all expensive to fix.

## Page 17 (printed page 17)

Roger’s First Check: Grab a flashlight and look under every sink for damp
spots, corrosion, or water stains. Don’t just glance—shine the light deep into
corners and behind pipes.
Cheap Fix: Tighten loose fittings, replace old washers, or swap out a
corroded hose yourself for under $20.
Call a Pro: If the leak is coming from old galvanized pipes or solder joints
and tightening doesn’t help, get a plumber before the damage spreads.
Money Saved: Catching a small leak early can save you $150-$600 or more
in water damage and mold cleanup.

Fix 8 — Read Water Stains Before You Open a Wall
The Problem: Water stains on walls or ceilings are warning signs, but tearing into
the wall without knowing what caused them leads to wasted time and money.
Why It Costs Money: Opening up drywall or plaster is a job itself. If you don’t
diagnose the source first, you’ll pay to fix walls and still have the leak or moisture
problem afterward.
Roger’s First Check: Look closely at the shape, edges, and color of stains.
A ring stain usually means a slow leak overhead. A fuzzy or cracked area
might be from condensation or a past problem.
Cheap Fix: Use a moisture meter or your hand to check for wetness around
the stain. If dry, monitor it weekly before opening walls.
Call a Pro: If you find active leaks or suspect plumbing inside the wall, get a
plumber or leak detection expert before demolition.
Money Saved: Avoiding unnecessary wall repair can save $500-$2,500,
depending on wall size and finish.

Fix 9 — Use Your Water Meter to Catch Hidden Leaks
The Problem: Hidden leaks inside walls or under floors can run continuously,
wasting water and causing damage without obvious signs.
Why It Costs Money: The longer a leak runs, the worse the damage and the
higher your water bill. Waiting for visible signs can cost you big.

## Page 18 (printed page 18)

Roger’s First Check: Turn off all water fixtures and appliances. Watch your
water meter for several minutes—if it moves, you’ve got a leak somewhere.
Cheap Fix: Check toilets for silent leaks using food coloring in the tank or
listen for drips. Replace flappers or valves yourself for $10-$30.
Call a Pro: Persistent leaks that you can’t locate or fix need a plumber with
leak detection gear.
Money Saved: Catching leaks early can save water bills and damage repair
costs from $150 up to several thousand.

Shopping

have invites returns, wrong parts, and wasted trips.
Why It Costs Money: Buying the wrong valve or fitting means extra trips, returns,
and sometimes paying for professional help to fix your mistakes.

pipe threads, shutoffs, and connections. Note any markings or sizes you see.
Cheap Fix: Use your phone; it’s free and saves you from guessing. Bring

Call a Pro: If you’re unsure about compatibility, ask a pro or the plumbing
counter before buying. It’s cheaper than wrong parts.
Money Saved: Avoiding wrong purchases can save $20-$100 per trip, plus

Fix 11 — Start an Old-House Repair Log
The Problem: Old houses have layers of fixes, some forgotten or undocumented.
Without records, you risk repeating repairs or missing patterns.
Why It Costs Money: You might replace something that was just fixed, overlook
recurring issues, or fail to track part life cycles.

Chapter 3 — Drips That Turn Into
Bills
Old houses and water leaks go together like old wood and nails—sometimes a
good fit, but often a pain in the behind. A faucet drip isn’t just a little annoying
sound; it’s a slow leak that can cost you in ways you might not see right off the
bat. Water stains on your sink or countertop, rotted wood under the cabinet, or
even mold hiding in dark corners—these are the real expenses that pile up after
ignoring a simple drip. And those drip-drip sounds? They’re the house’s way of
begging for a fix before that cheap little washer turns into a service call you don’t
want.
This chapter covers Fixes 13 through 18, all about stopping those leaks before
they become money pits. You’ll learn how to handle faucet drips, clean aerators
that block water flow, tighten loose faucets, and even test for sneaky slow leaks.
Knowing when to replace a faucet versus when a repair will do can save you a
bundle, especially in an old house where parts and setups aren’t always standard.
Roger’s Rule:
Don’t let a drip turn into damage. Fix it fast, fix it right, and save yourself the
headache—and the bill.

Fix 13 — Stop a Faucet Drip Before Replacing the Faucet
The Problem: A faucet dripping after you close it is usually a worn-out washer or
O-ring inside the faucet. In old houses, those rubber parts dry out or get brittle,
causing leaks that sound like a leaky roof on a rainy night.
Why It Costs Money: The drip wastes water—sometimes a surprising amount—
and constant moisture can stain sinks or cabinets, leading to costly repairs down
the line. Plus, if you call a plumber for a faucet that just needs a simple washer
change, you’re paying way more than you should.

## Page 24 (printed page 24)

Roger’s First Check: Shut off the water under the sink and take apart the
faucet handle to inspect the washer and O-rings.
Cheap Fix: Replace the washer and O-rings with a faucet repair kit from your
local hardware store. It’s usually under $10, and most kits include parts for
common faucet types.
Call a Pro: If the faucet drips even after you’ve swapped washers or if the
faucet is old and corroded beyond repair, it’s time to call a plumber.
Money Saved: $75-$250 by avoiding a full faucet replacement or
unnecessary service call.

Fix 14 — Clean an Aerator Before Blaming Water Pressure
The Problem: Low water pressure at the faucet often gets blamed on the main line
or plumbing issues, but in old houses, the culprit is often a clogged aerator.
Mineral deposits and gunk build up in the tiny screen where water comes out.
Why It Costs Money: Calling a plumber for low pressure when all you need is to
clean the aerator wastes money and time. Plus, a clogged aerator wastes water and
makes chores take longer, which can cost you in frustration and utility bills.
Roger’s First Check: Unscrew the aerator from the tip of the faucet spout—
usually just a twist—and inspect for debris or mineral buildup.
Cheap Fix: Soak the aerator in vinegar for an hour or two, then scrub with an
old toothbrush. Rinse and reinstall.
Call a Pro: If cleaning doesn’t improve pressure and multiple faucets are
affected, it’s time to get a plumber to check the pipes.
Money Saved: $50-$150 by handling it yourself and avoiding a service call.

Fix 15 — Fix the Leak Where the Faucet Meets the Sink
The Problem: Water leaking around the base of the faucet often means worn
gaskets or loose mounting nuts under the sink. In old houses, shifting sinks or
corroded parts can make these leaks more common.
Why It Costs Money: Water pooling under the sink causes wood rot, mold, and
damage to cabinets—expensive headaches that no one wants. Ignoring a leak here
can turn a small fix into a big repair.

## Page 25 (printed page 25)

Roger’s First Check: Look under the sink for moisture or water stains
around the faucet mounting hardware.
Cheap Fix: Tighten the mounting nuts carefully—don’t overtighten or you’ll
crack the sink. Replace worn gaskets or use plumber’s putty or silicone caulk
around the faucet base if needed.
Call a Pro: If tightening doesn’t stop the leak or if the sink is cracked, call a
plumber or handyman.
Money Saved: $100-$300 by avoiding cabinet damage and mold remediation.

Fix 16 — Tighten a Loose Faucet the Right Way
The Problem: A wobbly faucet isn’t just annoying; it can loosen water connections
and lead to leaks. Old sinks and counters settle over time, and faucet nuts can
back off.
Why It Costs Money: Loose faucets can cause leaks behind the scenes, leading to
water damage. Plus, a loose faucet is a safety hazard—someone can get hurt if it
suddenly shifts or breaks.
Roger’s First Check: Check the faucet’s stability by gently rocking it. Then,
look under the sink at the mounting nuts holding it in place.
Cheap Fix: Use the right-size basin wrench to snug the mounting nuts. Don’t
overtighten—you want firm, not broken.
Call a Pro: If you can’t access the nuts or if tightening doesn’t help, get a
plumber to avoid risking damage.
Money Saved: $75-$200 by preventing leaks and avoiding damage.

Fix 17 — Know When a Faucet Is Worth Replacing
The Problem: Sometimes a faucet is so old or corroded that even repairs won’t fix
leaks or performance issues. Old brass or chrome finishes may pit or crack, and
internal parts may be obsolete.
Why It Costs Money: Holding on to a faucet past its prime can waste water and
cause damage. Also, finding replacement parts for vintage faucets can be expensive
or impossible, leading to emergency replacements.

## Page 26 (printed page 26)

Roger’s First Check: Inspect the faucet for corrosion, cracks, or parts you
can’t replace. If repairs are frequent, it’s time to consider replacement.
Cheap Fix: Choose a good-quality faucet with a warranty and standard
fittings to make future repairs easier.
Call a Pro: Have a plumber install the new faucet to ensure proper sealing
and no leaks.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by avoiding repeated repairs and water damage.

Fix 18 — Use the Paper-Towel Test for Slow Sink Leaks
The Problem: Slow leaks can hide in plain sight, and sometimes you don’t notice
them until there’s visible damage. A tiny leak under the sink might only show as
dampness or a musty smell.
Why It Costs Money: Slow leaks lead to wood rot, mold growth, and mildew—
nasty stuff that can cost thousands to fix and is bad for your health.
Roger’s First Check: Place dry paper towels around pipes, joints, and fittings under the sink. Check them after a day or two for moisture.
Cheap Fix: Tighten any loose fittings with a wrench and replace worn
washers or tape on threaded joints.
Call a Pro: If the leak persists or pipes are corroded, call a plumber before
damage spreads.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call and $300-$1,000 in damage
control.

Before you move on, take a flashlight and get under your sinks tonight. Look for
drips, moisture, or loose fittings. Grab a wrench and tighten what you can—it’s
free and fast. If you see water stains or damp paper towels, that’s your house
telling you it’s time to act. These little leaks seem harmless, but in an old house,
they’re like termites: quiet, slow, and costly if ignored. Fix the small stuff now,
and you might dodge a major water damage bill later.

## Page 29 (printed page 29)

Chapter 4 — Supply Lines,
Shutoffs, and Cheap Parts That
Prevent Floods
Leaks in an old house usually start small and sneak up on you. Most often, they’re
from flexible supply lines, shutoff valves that won’t turn, or corroded fittings you
never gave a second thought. These parts aren’t glamorous, but they’re the weak
links that can flood your kitchen or bathroom without warning. The fixes in this
chapter—Fixes 19 through 24—focus on these everyday trouble spots. A little
attention here can save you from a soaked floor, damaged cabinets, or worse, a full
flood that ruins walls and floors.
Old supply lines made of rubber don’t last forever. When they fail, water doesn’t
trickle—it gushes. Shutoff valves, especially the old compression or gate valves,
sometimes look fine but are ready to snap or leak. You don’t want to find that out
the hard way during an emergency. And when you tighten a packing nut instead of
replacing a whole valve, you can avoid a pricey plumber visit. But knowing when
to quit forcing a stuck valve can save you from causing a bigger mess.
This chapter will also remind you to replace the toilet supply line before you take
off on vacation and to check washing machine hoses regularly. These are cheap
parts that rarely get noticed until they fail. If you use the simple inspection habits
and quick fixes here, you’ll dodge a lot of headaches and save yourself from
emergency calls that can cost hundreds or thousands.
Roger’s Rule:
Cheap parts fail slow but flood fast. Don’t wait for a drip to start your inspection.

Fix 19 — Replace Rubber Supply Lines Before They Burst
The Problem: Those flexible rubber supply lines under sinks and toilets are cheap,
but they age like fruit left out in the sun. They crack, bulge, and finally burst,
usually when you least expect it. In an old house, the water pressure and mineral
deposits can speed up their breakdown.

## Page 30 (printed page 30)

Why It Costs Money: When a line bursts, it can flood cabinets, soak floors, and
cause damage that runs into the hundreds or thousands to fix. Plus, emergency
plumber calls after hours are never cheap.
Roger’s First Check: Look under every sink and behind toilets. Feel the
lines for softness, bulges, or cracks. If a line is older than five years or looks
tired, replace it.
Cheap Fix: Swap out rubber lines for braided stainless steel ones. They cost
a few bucks more but last decades longer and handle pressure better.
Call a Pro: If the shutoff valve is seized or the fittings are corroded, don’t
force it. Call a plumber to avoid breaking pipes or valves.
Money Saved: Avoid one emergency call and water damage—potentially
$500 to $2,500 saved.

Fix 20 — Spot a Failing Shutoff Valve Before It Snaps
The Problem: Old shutoff valves can corrode inside and out. They might still turn,
but the metal is weak and can snap off when you try to shut the water quickly.
That leaves you with no way to stop a leak until the main is shut off.
Why It Costs Money: A snapped valve can cause flooding and damage. Replacing
a valve after it breaks is more expensive than preemptive replacement.
Roger’s First Check: Test each shutoff valve by turning it on and off gently.
Feel for stiffness, grinding, or leaks around the stem.
Cheap Fix: Replace old valves showing corrosion or stiffness with new
quarter-turn ball valves. They cost $15 to $30 and are more reliable.
Call a Pro: If you’re dealing with corroded pipes or valves that won’t move at
all, get a plumber to avoid breaking copper or steel lines.
Money Saved: Prevent one valve snap and flood scenario—$150 to $600
saved.

Fix 21 — Tighten a Packing Nut Instead of Replacing a Valve
The Problem: Sometimes a valve leaks at the stem, dripping water slowly. Many
homeowners think the entire valve needs replacing, but often the packing nut just
needs tightening.

## Page 31 (printed page 31)

Why It Costs Money: Replacing a valve costs more and takes longer, especially if
pipes are old and fittings are stuck. Tightening a packing nut is quick and cheap.
Roger’s First Check: Look for drips or wet spots around the valve stem. Use
an adjustable wrench to tighten the packing nut slightly—don’t overtighten or
you’ll make it worse.
Cheap Fix: Tighten the packing nut enough to stop drips. If that doesn’t
work, a new packing washer might help before replacing the valve.
Call a Pro: If tightening doesn’t stop the leak or the valve is too stiff to turn,
call a plumber. Forcing it could snap the valve.
Money Saved: Save $75 to $150 by avoiding a full valve replacement.

Fix 22 — Know When Not to Force an Old Valve
The Problem: Old valves that haven’t been turned in years can seize up. Trying to
force them might break the valve or pipe, causing leaks or floods.
Why It Costs Money: Breaking a valve or pipe means bigger repairs and possibly
emergency service calls.
Roger’s First Check: If a valve won’t budge with moderate force, don’t
muscle it. Try applying penetrating oil and wait a day before trying again.
Cheap Fix: Use penetrating oil on stuck valves once or twice a year as
preventive maintenance.
Call a Pro: If the valve remains stuck after oiling, call a plumber to replace it
safely.
Money Saved: Avoid pipe or valve breakage and emergency repairs—$200
to $1,000 saved.

Fix 23 — Replace a Toilet Supply Line Before Vacation
The Problem: Toilet supply lines are often ignored for years. They’re usually old
rubber or plastic and can burst when you’re away, flooding the bathroom.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage from a toilet line burst can ruin floors, walls,
and cause mold. Cleanup and repairs get pricey fast.

## Page 32 (printed page 32)

Roger’s First Check: Replace toilet supply lines every three to five years,
especially before leaving town.
Cheap Fix: Use braided metal supply lines for durability. They cost about $10
to $20 and are easy to install.
Call a Pro: If the shutoff valve is corroded or won’t turn, get a plumber to
replace it along with the line.
Money Saved: Avoid water damage and emergency calls—$300 to $1,200
saved.

Fix 24 — Check Washing Machine Hoses Before They Fail
The Problem: Washing machine hoses can crack, bulge, or split, especially older
rubber ones. A burst hose can flood your laundry room in minutes.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage and ruined appliances add up. Plus, the
cleanup can be a big hassle.
Roger’s First Check: Inspect hoses every six months. Look for cracks, stiffness, or bulges. Replace any suspect hoses immediately.
Cheap Fix: Switch to stainless steel braided hoses for better durability.
Call a Pro: If the hose connections are corroded or the water supply valves
are stuck, call a plumber.
Money Saved: One avoided flood can save $500 to $2,000 or more.

Before You Move On
Take a flashlight and get under every sink and behind every toilet in your home
right now. Feel the supply lines, look at shutoff valves, and check for corrosion or
leaking. Keep a simple inspection card nearby to note when you last replaced lines
or tightened packing nuts. Old houses don’t give many second chances once a part
fails; a few minutes of regular checking can save you a flood of trouble and a big
hit to your wallet. Don’t wait until your vacation or after you spot water on the
floor—get ahead of these cheap, easy fixes today.

## Page 35 (printed page 35)

Chapter 5 — Water Damage Clues
in Old Houses
Water sneaks into old houses like a thief in the night. You won’t always hear or
see it right away. Instead, it leaves signs—stains on your ceiling, a soft spot near
the toilet, or a musty smell that won’t quit. The tricky part is spotting these clues
early before water turns into rot, mold, or a full-blown mess that costs thousands
to fix. This chapter covers Fixes 25 through 30, all about finding water damage
hiding in plain sight.
Old houses have more joints, cracks, and old materials that don’t shed water like
new ones do. That means even a small leak can cause big problems if you don’t
catch it. I’m going to walk you through practical ways to trace leaks, check for
hidden damage, and test toilets for sneaky drips. These are simple checks and fixes
you can do yourself before calling in a pro and opening your wallet.
Water damage doesn’t just show up overnight; it leaves clues. Sometimes it’s a
ceiling stain, sometimes a soft floor near the toilet flange, or a smell that tells you
something’s wrong behind the walls. If you pay attention and act early, you’ll keep
the damage small and the repair bills manageable. This chapter aims to help you
spot those clues so you don’t get blindsided.
Roger’s Rule: Never guess at a leak’s source. Follow the water’s trail carefully. A wrong diagnosis can cost you more than the leak itself.

Fix 25 — Trace a Ceiling Stain Without Guessing
The Problem: That brown stain on your ceiling might look like an old coffee spill,
but it’s usually water. The tricky part? Water can travel sideways inside the ceiling
or wall before it shows up. If you just patch the stain, you’re ignoring the real
leak.
Why It Costs Money: If you fail to track the leak’s source, water keeps soaking
wood and plaster. That leads to mold, rot, and sometimes electrical shorts. Repair
bills balloon fast when ceilings collapse or framing has to be replaced.

## Page 36 (printed page 36)

Roger’s First Check: Grab a flashlight and look for dampness or peeling
paint near the stain. Check above the ceiling—if you can access the attic,
look for wet insulation or drips. Follow the water trail uphill since water runs
downhill.
Cheap Fix: Tighten plumbing fittings or replace a worn pipe section you find.
If it’s a roof leak, sealing or patching the shingles might do the trick.
Call a Pro: If the leak source is in a wall cavity or involves old plumbing you
can’t reach, bring in a plumber or roofer. Don’t gamble on guesswork.
Money Saved: Catching a ceiling leak early can save you $500 to $2,500 in
repairs.

Fix 26 — Check a Toilet Base Before It Rots the Floor
The Problem: Old toilets can leak where they meet the floor. That wax seal under
the bowl wears out or shifts, letting water seep under and soften subflooring before
you notice.
Why It Costs Money: Soft floors need plywood replaced, and if rot spreads to
joists, the job gets expensive fast. Plus, a loose toilet risks cracking the porcelain
or causing bad odors.
Roger’s First Check: Feel the floor around the toilet base for softness or
wobble. Look for water stains or discoloration on the floor or molding.
Cheap Fix: Replace the wax ring seal and tighten bolts. This usually takes a
couple of hours and a new wax ring costs under $10.
Call a Pro: If the floor is already soft or you see mold, call a plumber or
contractor. They’ll inspect the subfloor and joists for damage.
Money Saved: Fixing a toilet seal early can save $150 to $600 or more in
floor repairs.

Fix 27 — Find Hidden Sink-Cabinet Damage Early
The Problem: Water leaks under kitchen or bathroom sinks are common and often
hidden behind cabinet walls. Slow drips ruin wood, cause mold, and rot the cabinet
bottom before you smell anything.
Why It Costs Money: Replacing cabinet bases, mold remediation, and repairing
wall damage can easily run into the thousands once rot sets in.

## Page 37 (printed page 37)

Roger’s First Check: Open cabinet doors and look for water stains, swollen
wood, or a damp smell inside. Touch the bottom panel for softness or stickiness.
Cheap Fix: Tighten faucet supply lines and drain fittings. Replace worn
washers or old plastic parts before they crack.
Call a Pro: If you find dark mold or soft wood, call a plumber and possibly a
carpenter. They can fix leaks and replace damaged cabinetry.
Money Saved: Catching leaks early can save $200 to $1,000 in repair costs.

Fix 28 — Use the Food-Coloring Test for Toilet Tank Leaks
The Problem: Old toilet tanks sometimes leak internally into the bowl, causing
constant water flow and high bills. You don’t see it because the water just runs
down the drain.
Why It Costs Money: A running toilet wastes water and can increase your water
bill by hundreds over a year. Plus, it stresses the fill valve, leading to more repairs.
Roger’s First Check: Put a few drops of food coloring in the toilet tank and
wait 15 minutes without flushing. If colored water seeps into the bowl, you’ve
got a leak.
Cheap Fix: Replace the flapper valve or flush valve gasket. Parts are cheap
—usually under $15—and the swap takes minutes.
Call a Pro: If the tank cracks or the flush mechanism is corroded, call a
plumber.
Money Saved: Fixing a running toilet can save $75 to $250 per year in water
bills.

Fix 29 — Catch Tub and Shower Caulk Failures Before Wall
Damage
The Problem: Old caulk around tubs and showers cracks or peels, letting water
seep behind tiles or walls. This leads to rot and mold behind the scenes.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage inside walls can mean tearing out drywall or
tile, mold remediation, and expensive repairs.

## Page 38 (printed page 38)

Roger’s First Check: Look for cracked, missing, or peeling caulk lines
around tubs and showers. Feel for soft spots on the wall near the caulk lines.
Cheap Fix: Remove old caulk with a scraper and apply fresh, mildew-resistant silicone caulk. It takes less than an hour and costs under $10.
Call a Pro: If you see tile coming loose or suspect wall damage, get a
contractor to inspect.
Money Saved: Early caulk repair can save $300 to $1,500 in wall and mold
damage.

Fix 30 — Know When a Musty Smell Means Stop and
Investigate
The Problem: That musty smell in your basement, closet, or behind walls is often
water damage hiding out of sight. Ignore it, and mold spreads fast.
Why It Costs Money: Mold removal and structural repairs can cost thousands, plus
mold affects your health.
Roger’s First Check: Follow the smell to the source. Use a moisture meter
or just a flashlight and your nose. Look for stains, peeling paint, or soft wood.
Cheap Fix: Fix leaks, improve ventilation, and use a dehumidifier to control
moisture.
Call a Pro: If mold covers large areas or you’re unsure about safety, hire a
mold remediation specialist.
Money Saved: Early mold control can save $500 to $3,000 or more.

Before you move on, take a flashlight and a notepad. Walk through your house
and look for any of the clues I’ve talked about—ceiling stains, soft floors, musty
smells, or cracked caulk. Write down what you find and prioritize fixes you can do
yourself. The sooner you track down water damage clues, the less you’ll pay in the
long run. Trust me, chasing water leaks without a plan is like chasing a ghost.
Stay sharp, follow the clues, and keep your old house dry.

## Page 42 (printed page 42)

Chapter 6 — Slow Drains and
Cheap Drain Wins
Slow drains are the plumbing equivalent of a nagging cough—you know something’s off, but you’re hoping it’ll clear up on its own. In old houses, drains get
sluggish more often than new ones because the pipes are narrower, older materials
corrode or warp, and years of soap scum, hair, and gunk pile up inside. Before
grabbing that bottle of chemical drain cleaner or calling an emergency plumber
who charges twice what you expected, take a breath and learn what kind of clog
you’re dealing with. This chapter covers Fixes 31 through 36, and I’ll show you
how to safely tackle these slow drains with the right tools and tricks that won’t
break the bank or make the problem worse.
You see, the key to saving money is to stop guessing and start diagnosing. Some
clogs are just surface-level blockages you can dislodge with a plunger or a simple
trap cleaning. Others need a little more muscle or a special tool but still don’t
require a pro’s bill. Avoiding chemical drain cleaners is a big part of that—those
products can eat away at old pipes and cause leaks that cost a lot more to fix than
a slow drain ever would. Knowing when to call a pro and when to roll up your
sleeves will keep your pipes happy and your wallet intact.
Roger’s Rule: Start small, stay safe, and don’t pour chemicals down old pipes.

Fix 31 — Stop Using Chemical Drain Cleaner in Old Pipes
The Problem: Chemical drain cleaners can seem like a quick fix for slow drains,
but in old pipes, they do more harm than good. The harsh chemicals eat away at
cast iron, galvanized steel, and even some older plastic pipes, causing leaks and
corrosion over time.
Why It Costs Money: Corroded pipes mean leaks, water damage, and sometimes
mold. Fixing those issues can run into the hundreds or thousands of dollars. What
started as a $10 bottle turns into a house-ruining headache.

## Page 43 (printed page 43)

Roger’s First Check: Look at your pipes—if they’re old metal or brittle
plastic, skip the chemical cleaners.
Cheap Fix: Use a plunger or a drain snake instead. These tools don’t harm
the pipes and often clear the clog fast.
Call a Pro: If the clog won’t budge with manual methods or if you see leaks
after using chemicals, call a plumber.
Money Saved: $150–$600 by avoiding pipe damage and emergency repairs.

Fix 32 — Use the Right Plunger for the Right Drain
The Problem: Using a standard cup plunger on a kitchen sink or a flange plunger
on a tub won’t get you anywhere. Each drain type needs a plunger designed for its
shape to create a real seal and push or pull the clog free.
Why It Costs Money: Using the wrong plunger wastes time and may push the
clog deeper, leading to more expensive repairs or a call-out fee.
Roger’s First Check: Identify your drain type—sink, toilet, or tub—and pick
the matching plunger.
Cheap Fix: Buy one plunger designed for your most common slow drain, and
keep it handy. Use steady, forceful plunges to shift the clog.
Call a Pro: If plunging doesn’t clear the drain after a few tries, or if water
backs up into other fixtures, it’s time for professional help.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call, $75–$250.

Fix 33 — Clear a Bathroom Sink Stopper the Easy Way
The Problem: Hair and soap gunk love to build up around bathroom sink stoppers,
turning a once-fast drainage spot into a slow-draining sink. The stopper often hides
the problem, so you don’t see the clog until water pools.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring this can lead to tougher clogs down the line, which
can require replacing pipes or expensive drain clearing.

## Page 44 (printed page 44)

Roger’s First Check: Remove the stopper—you usually just need to twist or
unscrew it—and check for hair and gunk.
Cheap Fix: Clean off the stopper and the drain opening with an old toothbrush or a wire hanger. Flush with hot water.
Call a Pro: If water still drains slowly after clearing the stopper, the clog
might be deeper.
Money Saved: $75–$200 by avoiding chemical cleaners and early pipe damage.

Fix 34 — Clean a P-Trap Without Turning It Into a Mess
The Problem: The P-trap under a sink catches debris that causes slow drains. But
if you don’t prepare for the inevitable water and gunk in the trap, cleaning it can
turn your cabinet floor into a swamp.
Why It Costs Money: Repairing water damage or replacing ruined cabinet shelves
adds up quickly. Plus, leaving a clog in the trap means paying for a plumber later.
Roger’s First Check: Put a bucket under the trap to catch water before
loosening the nuts.
Cheap Fix: Use channel-lock pliers or your hands (gloves recommended) to
unscrew the trap, dump the gunk, and rinse it out with hot water before reinstalling.
Call a Pro: If the trap is corroded, cracked, or leaks after cleaning, call a
plumber to replace it.
Money Saved: $150–$500 by preventing water damage and clearing clogs
yourself.

Fix 35 — Use Boiling Water Carefully and Know When Not To
The Problem: Pouring boiling water down a slow drain can help dissolve grease
and soap scum, but it can also damage older PVC or ABS pipes, and it won’t fix
clogs caused by hair or solids.
Why It Costs Money: Damaged pipes mean leaks and expensive repairs. Plus,
boiling water that doesn’t clear the clog wastes time and risks burns.

## Page 45 (printed page 45)

Roger’s First Check: Check what your drain pipe material is. If it’s metal,
boiling water is usually safe. If plastic, use caution or skip this step.
Cheap Fix: Pour boiling water slowly in stages, giving the hot water time to
work between pours.
Call a Pro: If the clog resists and slow drainage continues, or if you smell
sewer gas, it’s time for a professional inspection.
Money Saved: $75–$200 by avoiding pipe damage and ineffective DIY attempts.

Fix 36 — Flush a Slow Kitchen Drain Without Making It Worse
The Problem: Kitchen drains get slow because of grease, food scraps, and soap
buildup. Running water without breaking up the clog can make it worse by
washing debris deeper into the pipes or the septic system.
Why It Costs Money: A blocked kitchen drain can cause backups that lead to pipe
damage or costly service calls.
Roger’s First Check: Run hot water and use a plunger designed for sinks to
loosen the clog before flushing.
Cheap Fix: Remove and clean the sink’s strainer basket regularly. If the
drain is still slow, use a drain snake to pull out buildup.
Call a Pro: If the drain backs up into other fixtures or you smell sewer gas,
call a plumber immediately.
Money Saved: $150–$600 by preventing blockages and backups.

Before You Move On
Slow drains are a pain, but they rarely start as emergencies. Take a flashlight and
check your traps, stoppers, and drain openings regularly. Keep a plunger and small
drain snake on hand, and don’t let chemical cleaners near old pipes. If you spot
leaks or persistent slow drainage, don’t wait for things to get worse—call a pro.
Taking small, safe steps now can keep your drains flowing freely and your repair
bills low. Next time a slow drain sneaks up, you’ll know exactly which cheap fix
to try first.

## Page 48 (printed page 48)

Chapter 7 — Toilets: The
Cheapest Fixes in the House
Toilets get a bad rap for being the biggest pain in an old house. When they go
wrong, they can flood your floor, jam up mid-flush, or just run endlessly, wasting
water like there’s no tomorrow. What most folks don’t realize is these problems
usually come from tiny, cheap parts that wear out or get out of whack. Fixing
them yourself isn’t glamorous, but it’s one of the easiest ways to avoid a pricey
plumber’s visit.
This chapter covers Fixes 37 through 42 — all about the stuff inside your toilet
tank and the way it sits on the floor. These fixes are household jewels: a worn-out
flapper, a misadjusted chain, a fill valve that drips, or a toilet that rocks ever so
slightly can all cause headaches. But they’re also dirt cheap to fix if you catch
them early. A new flapper costs less than 10 bucks, and a wax ring under the
bowl is under 20.
If you let these problems slide, you’ll end up with water bills that make you
cringe or a bathroom floor that’s soaked, warped, or ready to give out. I’ve seen
plenty of old houses where a little bit of routine maintenance on a toilet saved the
homeowner hundreds—sometimes thousands—by stopping small leaks before
they became disasters.
Roger’s Rule: If a toilet’s acting up, don’t wait for it to flood the floor. Check the
tank parts first. Most of the time, those little plastic parts are the troublemakers.

Fix 37 — Fix a Running Toilet Before It Wastes a Month of
Water
The Problem: Your toilet keeps running after a flush, sometimes for hours. You
might hear that faint trickle or even the loud whoosh of water filling the tank constantly.
Why It Costs Money: A running toilet can waste up to 200 gallons of water a
day, translating into a higher water bill and unnecessary wear on your water heater.
Plus, constant running means components inside the tank are wearing out faster.

## Page 49 (printed page 49)

Roger’s First Check: Lift the tank lid and watch the flapper and fill valve as it
runs. A flapper that doesn’t seal or a fill valve stuck open is usually the culprit.
Cheap Fix: Replace the flapper or clean the valve seat where the flapper
seals. Both parts are cheap and easy to swap with a screwdriver and a little
patience.
Call a Pro: If the fill valve is acting up and you’re not comfortable replacing it
yourself, or if the tank has cracks or corrosion, get a plumber’s help.
Money Saved: $100 to $300 on water and repair costs, plus peace of mind.

Fix 38 — Replace a Flapper Before Calling a Plumber
The Problem: The flapper inside the tank is old, warped, or brittle, causing water
to leak from the tank into the bowl continuously.
Why It Costs Money: A leaking flapper leads to higher water bills and forces the
fill valve to run constantly, wearing it out prematurely.
Roger’s First Check: Shut off the water, flush the toilet, and inspect the
flapper closely for cracks, warping, or mineral buildup.
Cheap Fix: Buy a new flapper that matches your toilet model and snap it on.
It’s a simple swap that takes 10 minutes and a few bucks.
Call a Pro: If the flapper seat (where the flapper rests) is corroded or
damaged, or if the toilet model is unusual, a plumber might need to step in.
Money Saved: $75 to $150 on water bills and avoided plumber calls.

Fix 39 — Adjust the Chain That Ruins a Flush
The Problem: The chain connecting the flush handle to the flapper is too tight or
too loose, causing the flapper to not open fully or stay open.
Why It Costs Money: A bad chain adjustment can cause weak flushes, multiple
flushes per use, or continuous running, all of which increase water waste or lead to
clogs.

## Page 50 (printed page 50)

Roger’s First Check: Remove the tank lid and test the flush handle. Watch
how the chain moves the flapper.
Cheap Fix: Adjust the chain length so there’s just a little slack when the
flapper is closed—about half an inch. No tools needed, just patience.
Call a Pro: If the flush handle or lift arm is broken or corroded, a professional
replacement may be safer.
Money Saved: $50 to $100 by preventing wasted water and multiple flushes.

Fix 40 — Set the Tank Water Level Correctly
The Problem: The water in your tank is either too high and running into the
overflow tube or too low, resulting in weak flushes.
Why It Costs Money: Too much water wastes water every time the tank refills;
too little water means you’ll flush more than once or have frequent clogs.
Roger’s First Check: Look inside the tank for the water line. It should sit
about an inch below the top of the overflow tube.
Cheap Fix: Adjust the float on the fill valve. On older toilets, this might be a
metal arm you bend slightly; on newer ones, a plastic float cup you slide up
or down.
Call a Pro: If the fill valve is corroded, or you can’t get the water level right,
get professional help.
Money Saved: $90 to $200 on water bills and fewer clogs.

Fix 41 — Stop a Toilet From Rocking Before It Breaks the
Seal
The Problem: The toilet rocks when you sit down or push on it, often because the
floor is uneven or the mounting bolts are loose.
Why It Costs Money: A rocking toilet breaks the wax seal beneath it, leading to
leaks, water damage, and expensive bathroom floor repairs.

## Page 51 (printed page 51)

Roger’s First Check: Gently rock the toilet from side to side and front to
back to feel for movement.
Cheap Fix: Tighten the closet bolts carefully and use shims under the base
to stabilize the toilet. Use plastic or composite shims to avoid rot.
Call a Pro: If the floor is rotted or too uneven, or if you notice water damage,
call a plumber or handyman to replace the wax ring and fix the floor.
Money Saved: $200 to $1,000 by preventing leaks and floor damage.

Fix 42 — Know When a Toilet Leak Is Really a Floor Problem
The Problem: Water pools around the toilet base, but the leak isn’t from the tank
or bowl—it’s coming from underneath.
Why It Costs Money: A broken wax ring or damaged flange lets water seep into
the floor, causing rot, mold, and structural damage that can cost thousands to repair.
Roger’s First Check: Check for soft spots or discoloration on the floor
around the toilet base, and lift the toilet if safe to do so to inspect the wax
ring.
Cheap Fix: If the wax ring is old or squished, replace it along with the flange
if damaged. This requires removing the toilet but is doable with basic tools.
Call a Pro: If the floor is soft or moldy, or if you’re not comfortable removing
and reinstalling the toilet, call a plumber or carpenter.
Money Saved: $500 to $2,500 by stopping water damage early.

Before you move on, spend a few minutes watching your toilets. Lift the tank lid
and check the water level, listen for running water, and peek at the flapper. If you
catch those little leaks or misadjusted parts early, you’ll save a good chunk of cash
and headaches down the road. Toilets aren’t glamorous, but they’re the unsung
heroes of your bathroom’s health. Treat them right with small fixes, and they’ll
keep saving you money for years. Keep a spare flapper and some basic tools handy
—you never know when a quick fix will stop a flood in its tracks.

## Page 54 (printed page 54)

Chapter 8 — Odors, Disposals,
and Sewer Warning Signs
Old houses have a way of keeping their secrets in the corners where you least
want them—like that stubborn smell creeping up from the kitchen sink or the
bathroom that never quite feels fresh. This chapter covers Fixes 43 through 48,
and the goal here is simple: save you from wasting money chasing ghosts and
poking around in places that might lead to bigger headaches. Sometimes the fix is
a quick refill of a dry trap; other times it’s recognizing when your sewer line is
waving a red flag. And let’s not forget the garbage disposal—a kitchen tool that
can either be your best friend or your worst plumbing nightmare.
We’re talking about smells and drain troubles nobody wants to bring up at dinner,
but ignoring these signs can cost you. A little attention now can keep the water
flowing and the air smelling decent without needing a costly pro call or emergency
replacement. These fixes save money because they stop small problems before they
turn into giant bills. In old houses, that’s worth its weight in gold.
If you ever wonder where to start when your nose goes on high alert or your
disposal sounds like a dying robot, this chapter will steer you right. I’ll give you
practical steps you can take, when to give it a shot yourself, and when to put the
phone down and call a pro before things get worse.
Roger’s Rule:
If it smells like trouble or sounds like warning bells, don’t guess—check your
traps and vents first before digging deeper.

Fix 43 — Refill Dry P-Traps Before Chasing Ghost Odors
The Problem: Dry P-traps are the number one sneaky source of mysterious odors
in old houses. When water evaporates from these traps—usually under sinks or
floor drains—smelly sewer gases sneak up and make your house stink.
Why It Costs Money: People often call plumbers or buy expensive cleaners before
realizing the trap is just dry. That leads to unnecessary service calls or replacement
parts.

## Page 55 (printed page 55)

Roger’s First Check: Look under sinks, especially in seldom-used bathrooms or basement drains. Pour a cup of water down every drain to refill the
trap.
Cheap Fix: Keep a spray bottle handy with water to refresh traps every few
weeks, especially in guest bathrooms or unused drains.
Call a Pro: If the smell persists after refilling traps, or you suspect broken or
cracked pipes around the traps.
Money Saved: $50-$150 on avoided calls and needless cleaner purchases.

Fix 44 — Clean a Garbage Disposal Without Damaging It
The Problem: Garbage disposals in old houses get gunked up with grease, food
scraps, and sometimes foreign objects, which cause bad smells and poor performance.
Why It Costs Money: Using harsh chemicals or hard tools can damage the disposal, leading to replacement or expensive repairs.
Roger’s First Check: Turn off power and check the disposal chamber. Run
cold water and grind small ice cubes with lemon peels to clean and freshen.
Cheap Fix: Regularly grind a handful of ice cubes followed by citrus peels or
a bit of baking soda to keep the disposal clean without chemicals.
Call a Pro: If the disposal jams, won’t reset, or leaks water.
Money Saved: $75-$250 by avoiding replacement or professional cleaning
services.

Fix 45 — Reset a Disposal Before Replacing It
The Problem: Sometimes the garbage disposal just stops working and people jump
straight to buying a new one. Often, it just needs a reset.
Why It Costs Money: New disposals run $100 to $300 plus installation. Resetting
can save you that cost and hassle.

## Page 56 (printed page 56)

Roger’s First Check: Look under the disposal for the reset button—a small
red or black button on the bottom. Press it after unplugging the unit.
Cheap Fix: Make sure the disposal isn’t jammed by manually turning the
blades with an Allen wrench before resetting.
Call a Pro: If the disposal hums but doesn’t grind, or if resetting doesn’t bring
it back to life.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by skipping replacement and professional labor.

Fix 46 — Recognize a Main Sewer Line Warning Sign
The Problem: Backups, slow drains all over the house, and gurgling toilets can
mean your main sewer line is clogged or damaged.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring these signs can lead to sewage backups into your
home and expensive emergency repairs.
Roger’s First Check: Notice if multiple drains are slow or if the basement
floor drain bubbles when toilets flush.
Cheap Fix: Avoid using water heavily until a professional inspects the line.
Call a Pro: Immediately if sewage backs up into your home or you smell
strong sewer gas near the foundation.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or thousands in cleanup and repairs.

Fix 47 — Know Why Tree Roots Love Old Sewer Lines
The Problem: Old clay or cast-iron sewer pipes are magnets for tree roots seeking
water and nutrients, causing blockages or pipe damage.
Why It Costs Money: Root damage can cause leaks and blockages requiring expensive pipe replacement or rooter services.

## Page 57 (printed page 57)

Roger’s First Check: Look for soggy patches in your yard, slow drains, or
gurgling sounds near trees.
Cheap Fix: Avoid planting large trees near sewer lines; have a professional
rooter service clear roots before they cause damage.
Call a Pro: If you suspect roots are in your sewer line or have recurring
backups.
Money Saved: $500-$2,500 by preventing or addressing root damage early.

Fix 48 — Make a Bathroom Fan and Vent Check Part of Drain
Diagnosis
The Problem: Poor bathroom ventilation can trap humid air and odors, making
your drains and bathroom smell worse.
Why It Costs Money: Replacing or upgrading ventilation after water damage or
mold growth is costly.
Roger’s First Check: Turn on the bathroom fan and listen—if it’s weak or
silent, clean or replace the fan.
Cheap Fix: Clean the fan grille and check for blocked vent pipes on the roof
to ensure airflow.
Call a Pro: For roof vent repairs or if you spot mold or water damage.
Money Saved: $100-$500 by preventing mold and moisture damage.

Before You Move On
If you’re smelling trouble or your drains just aren’t right, don’t start throwing
money at fancy cleaners or new disposals right away. First, check your traps and
make sure they have water in them. Next, give your disposal a quick reset and
clean with ice and lemon before calling for replacements. And if all your drains
seem sluggish or you’re getting weird gurgles, stop using water and call a pro
before things get nasty. Old houses don’t let you ignore these signs for long. A
little early attention can save you a big pile of cash and a bigger headache down
the road.

Possible chemical residue. Do not plunge or open traps until flushed safely; protect eyes and skin.
Gas-like near water heater
Do not troubleshoot casually. Leave area and call the gas utility or qualified professional if gas odor is suspected.
Moldy at disposal
Food film or splash-guard buildup. Clean gently; stop if water backs up into another fixture.
Sulfur only at hot water
Often points toward water heater anode/bacteria issue. Record age and symptoms before calling or servicing.
Stop-and-call threshold
If odor is paired with sewage, multiple slow fixtures, dizziness, gas-like smell, electrical risk, or recurring moisture, stop the DIY path and call qualified help.

## Page 62 (printed page 62)

Chapter 9 — Know What Your
Pipes Are Telling You
Old houses have stories in their walls, and some of the loudest storytellers are the
pipes. If you don’t know what you’re looking at, you’ll miss the clues that can
save you headaches and big repair bills. This chapter, covering Fixes 49 through
53, is all about reading your pipes like a pro—even if you’ve never picked up a
wrench. You don’t need a plumbing license, but you do need to know the difference between copper and galvanized, when corrosion means trouble, and when
you’re looking at something that should stay alone—like lead or asbestos.
The money-saving theme here is simple: early recognition stops small problems
from turning into $2,500 emergencies. I’m talking about catching pinhole leaks
before they flood your floor, spotting the rusty signs of old cast iron about to fail,
and understanding your noisy pipes without calling in a detective. You’ll also learn
why certain materials cost more over time and when you absolutely should not
mess with what you don’t know.
If you go through this chapter with a flashlight and a little grit, you’ll leave the
guesswork behind and know exactly when to tighten a fitting, when to replace a
pipe, and when to call in the pros for safety’s sake. Plus, you’ll get a solid feel for
the six common pipe types in old homes—think of it as a “Pipe Material
Identification Guide” in your head.
Roger’s Rule: If your pipes are whispering trouble, listen early. Don’t wait for a
flood to find out what they’re saying.

Fix 49 — Identify Copper, PEX, PVC, Galvanized, Cast Iron,
and Mystery Pipe
The Problem: Old houses often have a patchwork of pipe materials. Not knowing
what you’re dealing with leads to wasted time, wrong parts, and sometimes
dangerous assumptions.
Why It Costs Money: Using the wrong repair materials or techniques can cause
leaks or pipe damage, leading to costly callbacks or replacements. Plus, some pipes
just shouldn’t be touched without the right know-how.

## Page 63 (printed page 63)

Roger’s First Check: Shine a flashlight on your pipes and get familiar.
Copper is reddish and dulls with age; PEX is flexible and usually red, blue, or
white plastic tubing; PVC is white or cream plastic with smooth joints; galvanized pipe is steel with a dull gray finish and threaded joints; cast iron is heavy,
black, and usually found in drainage. If it looks weird or crumbly, it’s a
mystery pipe—don’t guess.
Cheap Fix: Label your pipes with masking tape and a sharpie once you
identify them. It makes future fixes easier and avoids buying wrong parts.
Call a Pro: When you find pipes you can’t identify or suspect are old lead or
cast iron, bring in a plumber who can test and advise replacement.
Money Saved: $50-$150 by avoiding wrong materials and unnecessary repairs.

Fix 50 — Spot Corrosion Before a Pin-Hole Leak Appears
The Problem: Corrosion doesn’t scream until it’s too late. Pinholes start small, but
they quickly turn into drips, then full leaks.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage from leaks leads to mold, rot, and structural
damage that can cost thousands to fix. Catching corrosion early means fixing or
replacing before disaster.
Roger’s First Check: Look for green or blue-green stains on copper, reddish
rust on galvanized, or flaky, rusty spots on cast iron. Check joints and places
under sinks or near water heaters.
Cheap Fix: Clean rusty spots with a wire brush and apply a corrosion-resistant paint or wrap with pipe repair tape designed for corrosion. This is a
temporary fix, but it buys you time.
Call a Pro: When corrosion is widespread or pinholes have appeared, a
plumber should assess whether you need a section replaced or a full system
upgrade.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by stopping leaks before water damage.

## Page 64 (printed page 64)

Fix 51 — Know Why Galvanized Pipe Makes Old Houses
Expensive
The Problem: Galvanized pipe was popular decades ago but now is a ticking time
bomb. It rusts inside, narrows water flow, and eventually leaks.
Why It Costs Money: Replacing galvanized pipe is expensive and invasive—but
ignoring it means low water pressure, leaks, and water damage. Plus, it can
contaminate your water supply.
Roger’s First Check: Tap the pipe; if it sounds dull and thick with scale
inside, that’s a bad sign. Look for rust streaks on walls and fittings. Low water
pressure in an old house often points to galvanized pipe clogging.
Cheap Fix: There’s no good cheap fix. You can try flushing your system to
dislodge scale, but it’s a short-term band-aid.
Call a Pro: Replacement is often the only real fix. A plumber can run new
copper or PEX alongside or replace old galvanized pipe, depending on the
job.
Money Saved: Avoid $500-$2,500 in water damage and corrosion-related
repairs by planning replacement before failure.

Fix 52 — Do Not Disturb Possible Lead or Asbestos Materials
The Problem: Some old pipes or pipe insulation may contain lead or asbestos.
Disturbing these can release harmful particles into your home.
Why It Costs Money: Cleaning up lead or asbestos contamination can cost thousands and pose serious health risks. Mistakes here aren’t just expensive—they’re
dangerous.
Roger’s First Check: Look for dull gray pipes with a smooth finish that don’t
look like steel; that could be lead. Asbestos insulation is old, crumbly, and
often wrapped around pipes with a paper-like texture. If you’re unsure, don’t
touch it.
Cheap Fix: Avoid DIY on suspect materials. Seal off areas temporarily and
keep kids and pets away.
Call a Pro: Call a certified hazardous materials contractor for testing and
removal. It’s not a place to save money by doing it yourself.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency cleanup can save thousands and
protect your family.

## Page 65 (printed page 65)

Fix 53 — Use Pipe Noise as a Clue, Not a Mystery
The Problem: Pipes bang, whistle, or drip, and most people ignore it or panic
without cause. Noise can tell you what’s wrong if you know what to listen for.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring noises can let small problems turn into big leaks or
damage. Overreacting means unnecessary service calls. Knowing the difference
saves time and money.
Roger’s First Check: Listen for knocking when you turn off faucets—water
hammer means loose pipes or missing air chambers. Whistling suggests a
clogged valve or narrowing pipe. Dripping means a leak or failing washer.
Cheap Fix: Install a water hammer arrestor or tighten pipe brackets to stop
banging. Replace washers in faucets to stop dripping noises.
Call a Pro: If noises persist or you suspect blockages inside pipes, call a
plumber to inspect and fix underlying problems.
Money Saved: $75-$250 by fixing noise-related issues before they cause
damage.

Before You Move On
Take a flashlight and spend some time getting familiar with your pipes. Label what
you can, note anything rusty or noisy, and keep an eye out for materials you don’t
recognize. Don’t poke at anything suspicious—if you think you’ve found lead or
asbestos, lock down the area and call a pro. Early recognition is your best defense,
and it’s often the difference between a quick fix and a costly emergency. Knowing
your pipes isn’t just about saving money—it’s about keeping your home safe and
sound for years to come.

## Page 68 (printed page 68)

Chapter 10 — Emergency Patches
and Temporary Saves
Leaks don’t wait for your schedule. You might spot a drip at midnight or during a
holiday when calling a plumber feels impossible. That’s when a good temporary
patch can save you from a flood, mold, or costly damage while you line up a
proper fix. This chapter covers Fixes 54 through 58, all about stopping leaks dead
in their tracks with smart, cautious moves.
Temporary fixes are not permanent repairs. If you treat them like a stopgap—not
a long-term solution—you’ll avoid bigger headaches and bigger bills. That means
knowing the right tools, like pipe repair clamps, and the right tricks, like using the
right type of tape or how to handle those pesky compression fittings that never
seem to seal just right. Plus, sometimes the best fix is a bucket, a towel, and a
quick photo before anything else happens.
If you rush a patch without knowing what you’re doing, you could end up making
the problem worse or missing signs that the pipe is failing beyond repair. So, let’s
talk about smart temporary saves that keep water where it belongs, not on your
floors or walls.
Roger’s Rule: Temporary fixes aren’t set-and-forget. Treat them like a smoke
alarm—useful, lifesaving, but you still need to replace the batteries and get a
real fix fast.

Fix 54 — Use a Pipe Repair Clamp the Right Way
The Problem: A sudden leak in an old pipe joint or a small crack can send water
gushing if left unchecked. You might grab a pipe clamp, but without proper
placement, it won’t seal, or worse, it’ll cause more damage.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage can ruin wood, drywall, and insulation fast.
A bad clamp job means you pay for cleanup and a rushed repair instead of just the
repair.

## Page 69 (printed page 69)

Roger’s First Check: Turn off the water first. Dry the pipe completely before
clamping. Clean the pipe’s surface with sandpaper or steel wool to help the
clamp seal.
Cheap Fix: Use a rubber strip under the clamp to cushion and seal the leak
area. Tighten the clamp enough to stop the drip but don’t crank it down hard
—old pipes are brittle.
Call a Pro: If the leak is near a joint or the pipe is heavily corroded, call a
plumber. A clamp is a patch, not a cure.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by avoiding water damage and emergency
plumber fees.

Fix 55 — Know What Tape Can and Cannot Fix
The Problem: When water leaks, your first instinct might be to grab duct tape or
electrical tape. Spoiler: most tapes won’t hold up against pressurized water in
pipes.
Why It Costs Money: Using the wrong tape wastes time and lets leaks worsen.
Then you pay for bigger repairs or a flood cleanup.
Roger’s First Check: Identify the leak’s size and location. Is it a slow drip or
a steady stream? Tapes aren’t for big leaks.
Cheap Fix: Use specialized plumbing repair tape, like silicone self-fusing
tape, for temporary sealing on small leaks or pinholes. Wrap tightly with
overlap and stretch.
Call a Pro: If the leak is bigger than a pinhole or the tape fails after an hour
or two, call a plumber.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or $75-$250 on emergency repairs.

Fix 56 — Stop a Small Compression-Fitting Drip Without
Over-Tightening
The Problem: Compression fittings on older pipes can drip over time. Most
homeowners turn the nut tighter and tighter, which strips threads or cracks the fitting.
Why It Costs Money: Over-tightening can cause bigger leaks or broken fittings,
forcing costly replacements.

## Page 70 (printed page 70)

Roger’s First Check: Turn off water, dry the fitting, then tighten the compression nut gently with a wrench—no more than a quarter turn past hand-tight.
Cheap Fix: If tightening doesn’t work, remove the fitting and check the olive
(the ring). Sometimes replacing the olive or adding a small piece of plumber’s
tape on threads helps.
Call a Pro: If it still leaks after replacing the olive or tape, get professional
help.
Money Saved: $75-$300 by preventing fitting damage and emergency repairs.

Fix 57 — Use a Bucket, Towel, and Photo Before Touching
Anything
The Problem: When you see water leaking, your first reaction might be to start
unscrewing or poking around. That can make the leak worse or cause water damage.
Why It Costs Money: Rushing in without containment or documentation can turn a
small drip into a flood or complicate insurance claims.
Roger’s First Check: Before touching anything, place a bucket or pan to
catch drips and lay down towels to protect floors. Snap a clear photo of the
leak’s source and surrounding area.
Cheap Fix: Contain the leak with buckets and towels, then schedule a repair
when you’re ready. The photo helps plumbers understand the problem before
arrival.
Call a Pro: If the leak is heavy or near electrical wiring, call emergency
services or a plumber immediately.
Money Saved: $75-$500 by preventing water damage and speeding up the
repair process.

Fix 58 — Recognize When a Patch Is Lying to You
The Problem: Sometimes a patch seems to hold, but the leak returns or worsens
because the underlying pipe is failing. These “band-aid” fixes give a false sense of
security.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring recurring leaks leads to bigger breaks or mold
damage, costing thousands more than a timely repair.

## Page 71 (printed page 71)

Roger’s First Check: If a patch leaks again within days or weeks, or if the
pipe feels soft or crusty under the patch, it’s time to replace the pipe or fitting.
Cheap Fix: Remove the old patch, dry the area, and try a fresh temporary
clamp or tape to buy time.
Call a Pro: For recurring leaks or seriously corroded pipes, call a plumber to
replace the damaged section.
Money Saved: $500-$2,500 by avoiding water damage and emergency repairs.

Before You Move On
When water’s involved, your first move can make all the difference. Don’t ignore a
drip, but don’t panic and make the problem worse. Get a bucket under the leak,
grab a towel, and take a photo. Then pick the right temporary fix—whether that’s
clamping, taping, or tightening a fitting just right. Keep in mind, these are just
band-aids, not cures. Stay safe by shutting off water when you can and calling a
pro if things get out of hand. If you keep these quick moves in your back pocket,
you’ll save yourself a headache—and maybe thousands.

Temporary Leak Response Card
Control damage first. Permanent repair comes next.

3 Dry + Photo

professional attention.
