## Page 74 (printed page 74)

Chapter 11 — Hose Bibbs,
Outdoor Lines, and Bad Previous
Repairs
If you own an old house, you know outdoor plumbing can be a sneaky money pit.
Hose bibbs—outdoor faucets—look simple enough, but that’s where the trouble
starts. They sit outside all year, get frozen, cracked, or just plain leaky. Then
there’s the whole mess of old pipes running through walls, sometimes patched up
with whatever was handy, and rarely done right. These hidden leaks and bad fixes
can soak your foundation, waste water, and rack up repair bills that hit you like a
hammer when you least expect it.
This chapter covers Fix 59 through Fix 64, all about catching those problems early
and handling them without draining your wallet. The key here is to get ahead of
freezing weather, know what’s behind the wall, and spot those “quick and dirty”
repairs before they turn into big headaches. A lot of homeowners don’t realize the
indoor shutoff valves for outdoor faucets exist, or that improper fittings can cause
more damage than good. We’ll cover those essentials, and I’ll help you take
pictures before calling a pro so you don’t get blind-sided by surprise fees.
Roger’s Rule:
Look before you dig—or drill—or call. Catch the trouble before it catches
you.

Fix 59 — Disconnect Hoses Before They Freeze the Wall
The Problem: Leaving hoses connected to hose bibbs when temperatures drop is a
fast way to crack the faucet or freeze water inside the wall. The frozen water
expands and can split pipes behind your siding.
Why It Costs Money: A cracked bibb or burst pipe means water leaks into your
wall or foundation, causing rot and expensive repairs. That’s often hundreds to
thousands in damage plus the hassle of wall repairs.

## Page 75 (printed page 75)

Roger’s First Check: Make sure all garden hoses are off and drained by the
start of cold weather. Feel around the bibb for any moisture or frost in early
winter.
Cheap Fix: Disconnect hoses, drain them, and use a bibb cover or insulated
foam sleeve to protect the faucet.
Call a Pro: If you see water stains inside or hear dripping behind a wall, call
a plumber to check for frozen or cracked pipes.
Money Saved: Avoids $150 to $600 in pipe and wall repairs.

Fix 60 — Find the Indoor Shutoff for Each Outdoor Faucet
The Problem: Many old houses have indoor shutoffs for hose bibbs, but owners
don’t know where they are. Without these, you can’t drain outdoor lines in winter
or isolate leaks quickly.
Why It Costs Money: No shutoff means water stays in outdoor pipes all winter,
risking freeze damage. Also, when leaks happen, shutting off water quickly limits
damage but you can’t do that without knowing where.
Roger’s First Check: Check your basement or crawlspace walls below each
outdoor faucet. Look for small valves with round or quarter-turn handles.
Cheap Fix: Mark shutoff valves with tape or tags so you won’t forget next
winter.
Call a Pro: If you don’t have an indoor shutoff, a plumber can install one,
saving you headaches down the road.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or freeze damage repair ($200–
$800).

Fix 61 — Spot a Leaking Hose Bibb Before It Soaks the
Foundation
The Problem: Hose bibbs often leak around the handle or at the pipe connection,
slowly dripping water where you can’t see it. This hidden leak can saturate your
foundation or crawlspace.
Why It Costs Money: Moisture near foundations invites rot, mold, and pest problems, all costly to fix. Plus, a dripping bibb wastes water and raises your bill.

## Page 76 (printed page 76)

Roger’s First Check: During a dry day, check the ground beneath each bibb
for wet spots or moss growth. Also, listen for dripping sounds.
Cheap Fix: Replace the hose bibb’s internal washer or cartridge; these parts
are cheap and easy to swap with a wrench.
Call a Pro: If the bibb is old, corroded, or the leak is at the pipe connection,
get a plumber to replace it properly.
Money Saved: Prevents $500 to $2,000 in foundation and mold repairs.

Fix 62 — Know When a SharkBite-Style Fitting Makes Sense
—and When It Does Not
The Problem: SharkBite and push-to-connect fittings are popular for quick fixes,
but they’re not always the best choice outdoors or in walls exposed to freezing or
movement.
Why It Costs Money: These fittings can fail if exposed to freezing or vibration,
causing leaks that are hard to spot and fix. Replacing failed SharkBites often costs
more than doing it right the first time.
Roger’s First Check: Look for SharkBite fittings on outdoor lines or inside
walls where freezing is possible.
Cheap Fix: Use SharkBites only on indoor, protected pipes or temporary
setups. For outdoor lines, soldered or threaded fittings are safer.
Call a Pro: If you find failed SharkBites leaking, have a plumber remove and
install proper fittings.
Money Saved: Avoids repeated leaks and repairs costing $150 to $600.

Fix 63 — Spot a Bad Previous Repair Before It Fails
The Problem: Old-house owners often inherit DIY or shortcut repairs that look
okay but are ticking time bombs. These include patched leaks with tape, glue, or
wrong-sized fittings.
Why It Costs Money: When these fixes fail, they can cause flooding, wall damage,
and emergency plumbing calls. The longer you wait, the worse the damage grows.

## Page 77 (printed page 77)

Roger’s First Check: Inspect all visible pipes for tape, mismatched fittings,
or glue joints that look sloppy or unusual.
Cheap Fix: If you feel comfortable, replace tape or glue repairs with proper
fittings and clamps.
Call a Pro: For anything behind walls or if you spot corrosion or cracks, call a
plumber before it fails.
Money Saved: Spotting bad repairs early can save $500 to $2,500 in
emergency repairs.

Fix 64 — Take the Right Photos Before Asking for a Repair
Quote
The Problem: When you call a plumber to fix outdoor line issues, not having clear
photos of the bibb, shutoffs, and visible piping can mean extra trips and higher
charges.
Why It Costs Money: Without good photos, plumbers may need to come twice or
charge more for diagnostics and travel.
Roger’s First Check: Use your phone to snap clear photos showing the outdoor faucet, nearby shutoff valve, and any suspicious spots like tape or corrosion.
Cheap Fix: Send these photos when you request quotes or schedule repairs
to give the plumber a head start.
Call a Pro: This step is your own prep; no pro needed here.
Money Saved: Can save $75 to $250 by avoiding extra calls or guesswork.

Before You Move On
Get outside before the next freeze hits and take a slow walk around your house
with a flashlight and your phone. Find every hose bibb and trace the pipe back
inside. Locate those indoor shutoff valves—I promise they’re there somewhere.
Disconnect hoses, snap photos, and mark what you find. This little bit of
homework can pay off big the moment cold weather rolls in or if you notice a
drip. Don’t wait for an emergency to remind you that outdoor plumbing isn’t just
for watering the lawn—it’s a hidden risk zone in every old house.

## Page 82 (printed page 82)

Chapter 12 — Water Heater Fixes
That Delay Replacement
Water heaters are like that cranky old uncle who gives you warnings before losing
it completely. They rarely fail without tossing out signs first—strange noises, slow
heating, or little leaks that whisper “fix me.” Trouble is, many folks ignore these
hints until the tank bursts or the pilot light goes out for good, and then it’s a mad
scramble for a replacement. That’s where this chapter comes in. Fixes 65 through
70 cover the practical stuff that keeps your water heater running longer and your
wallet from taking a hit.
In old houses, water heaters have been through the wringer: hard water, outdated
parts, and years without proper upkeep. Sediment builds up, anode rods dissolve,
and safety valves get tired. These issues don’t just cause inefficiency—they turn a
manageable repair into a costly replacement. Catching problems early, like draining
sediment or checking the T&P valve, can delay the day you have to shop for a
new unit. And knowing when you’re throwing good money after bad helps you
avoid wasting your hard-earned cash on a fix that won’t last.
This chapter’s practical fixes will help you read the signals your water heater
sends, nip problems in the bud, and handle maintenance like a pro—even if
plumbing isn’t your favorite hobby. Along the way, you’ll want to keep a flashlight handy and maybe sketch your own version of a Water Heater Maintenance
Map to keep track of what you’ve done and what needs doing.
Roger’s Rule: Water heaters don’t usually die overnight. Listen to the clues,
keep them clean, and replace parts before the whole tank turns into a flood
zone.

Fix 65 — Find the Water Heater Age Before Spending Money
The Problem: You don’t want to throw money at an old water heater that’s just a
few months from quitting. Without knowing its age, you might end up repairing a
unit that’s ready for retirement.

## Page 83 (printed page 83)

Why It Costs Money: Repairs on a water heater near the end of its lifespan often
don’t stick. That means paying twice—once for the fix and again for the replacement.
Roger’s First Check: Look for the serial number on the tank’s label. Usually,
the manufacturing date is coded in the first few digits. If you can’t read it, take
a photo and check online or ask a local plumber.
Cheap Fix: Once you know the age, you can decide if it’s worth flushing
money into repairs or budgeting for a replacement instead.
Call a Pro: If the label is missing or you’re unsure what the numbers mean, a
plumber can identify the age for you and advise on the unit’s expected
lifespan.
Money Saved: Knowing the age ahead can save you $150-$600 by avoiding
unnecessary repairs on a failing heater.

Fix 66 — Drain Sediment Before It Eats Efficiency
The Problem: Sediment, like sand and minerals, settles at the bottom of the tank,
making your water heater work overtime. This slows heating and can cause noise
or damage.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring sediment buildup wastes energy and shortens the
tank’s life, leading to higher utility bills and earlier replacement.
Roger’s First Check: Turn off the heater and let it cool a bit. Attach a garden
hose to the drain valve and let a few gallons flush out. If the water looks gritty
or rusty, you’ve got sediment.
Cheap Fix: Flushing the tank once a year keeps sediment from building up.
It takes a few minutes and saves wear and tear.
Call a Pro: If the drain valve is stuck or you’re unsure how to safely flush the
tank, call a plumber.
Money Saved: Flushing sediment can save $100-$300 yearly on energy bills
and delay tank replacement by years.

## Page 84 (printed page 84)

Fix 67 — Check the Anode Rod Before the Tank Rusts Out
The Problem: The anode rod is a sacrificial piece of metal inside the tank that
attracts corrosion so the tank doesn’t rust. When it’s gone, the tank starts to fail.
Why It Costs Money: Replacing a corroded tank is a big expense. Replacing the
anode rod is a fraction of that and can extend your tank’s life by years.
Roger’s First Check: Turn off the water and power. Unscrew the anode rod
on top of the tank—it looks like a thick metal rod—and inspect it. If it’s less
than half an inch thick or coated in crust, it’s time to replace.
Cheap Fix: Buy a new anode rod at any hardware store and screw it back in.
It usually takes less than an hour.
Call a Pro: If you don’t have the right wrench or the rod is stuck, a plumber
can swap it safely without damaging the tank.
Money Saved: Replacing the anode rod costs $20-$50 and can save $500-$2,000 by avoiding premature tank failure.

Fix 68 — Understand the T&P Valve Without Playing Around
The Problem: The Temperature and Pressure (T&P) valve is your water heater’s
safety valve. If it fails, pressure can build up dangerously, risking a tank explosion.
Why It Costs Money: A faulty T&P valve can cause leaks or, worse, a catastrophic failure. Replacing it before it fails prevents costly water damage and safety hazards.
Roger’s First Check: Never mess with the valve without turning off power
and water first. Lift the lever carefully—water should flow freely and stop
once released. If it sticks or drips after reset, it’s time for replacement.
Cheap Fix: T&P valves are inexpensive and can be replaced by handy
homeowners who know the basics.
Call a Pro: If you’re unsure or notice corrosion around the valve, have a
plumber replace it to ensure safety.
Money Saved: Replacing a T&P valve early can avoid thousands in water
damage and emergency repairs.

## Page 85 (printed page 85)

Fix 69 — Check for Leaks at the Water Heater Before They
Become Floods
The Problem: Small drips can turn into floods. Leaks at fittings, valves, or the tank
itself are often first noticed as puddles or rust stains.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring leaks wastes water, causes damage, and often
signals a tank failure coming soon.
Roger’s First Check: Inspect around the base of your heater monthly. Look
for puddles, wet insulation, or rust. Listen for dripping sounds.
Cheap Fix: Tighten loose fittings or replace old hose connectors before they
fail completely.
Call a Pro: If the tank itself is leaking or you see corrosion on the tank, call a
plumber immediately.
Money Saved: Catching leaks early can save $500-$2,500 by avoiding flood
damage or emergency replacement.

Fix 70 — Know When Replacement Is Smarter Than Repair
The Problem: Sometimes your water heater is just done. Repairing a 15-year-old
tank with multiple issues isn’t always the best move.
Why It Costs Money: Spending hundreds on repairs for an old, inefficient heater
wastes money better spent on a modern, efficient replacement.
Roger’s First Check: If your heater is over 10 years old, has recurring leaks,
rusty water, or strange noises, start budgeting for a new one.
Cheap Fix: Regular maintenance extends life, but don’t throw good money
after bad—plan ahead.
Call a Pro: A plumber can inspect and give you the lowdown on whether
fixes are worth it or replacement is smarter.
Money Saved: Avoid costly emergency replacements and high energy bills
by choosing replacement at the right time—savings vary but can top $1,000.

Before You Move On
Water heaters are workhorses you depend on every day, and they talk if you listen.
Take a flashlight and check your heater right now—find its age, drain a bit of
sediment, or just look for leaks. Mark what you find on a simple map or note for

## Page 86 (printed page 86)

yourself. That small habit can save you from a flood or a surprise replacement
down the road. Don’t wait for your hot water to turn cold before you act. A little
regular attention here keeps the headache—and the emergency calls—away.

## Page 89 (printed page 89)

Chapter 13 — Basement, Crawl
Space, and Moisture Saves
Old basements and crawl spaces are like the secret diaries of your house—they
tell you everything you need to know about water, humidity, and what’s lurking in
the shadows. Ignore them, and you’re asking for rot, mold, pests, and foundation
headaches that can drain your wallet faster than a busted pipe. This chapter covers
Fixes 71 through 76, all about spotting moisture trouble before it turns into an
expensive disaster.
Basements and crawl spaces in old houses often weren’t built to today’s moisture
standards. They tend to be damp, drafty, and cold, making them prime spots for
issues that start small but grow big—and costly. You don’t need fancy gadgets to
catch these problems early. Sometimes, your nose, a humidity gauge, or a simple
visual check will tell you more than a thousand words.
When you catch moisture problems early, you save money on repairs and keep
your home healthier. These fixes focus on practical checks and steps you can do
yourself, plus when to bring in a pro. The key is to stay ahead of moisture,
because once it gets into framing or your foundation, you’re looking at thousands
of dollars in repairs and a lot of headaches.
Roger’s Rule: When it comes to basement and crawl space moisture, trust your
senses first—especially your nose—and act before you see the damage.

Fix 71 — Use the Nose Test in Basements and Crawl Spaces
The Problem: Musty, damp smells are often the first sign that moisture is sticking
around where it shouldn’t be. Old houses with dirt floors or poor ventilation tend
to trap humidity, creating a breeding ground for mold and rot.
Why It Costs Money: Mold and rot lead to structural damage, can wreck stored
belongings, and sometimes trigger health issues that end up costing on top of repairs.

## Page 90 (printed page 90)

Roger’s First Check: Walk into your basement or crawl space after a rainy
day or a humid week. Take a deep breath. That earthy, stale smell? It’s your
early warning.
Cheap Fix: Improve airflow by opening vents or installing a simple fan. Use a
dehumidifier if you spot persistent dampness. Remove wet or moldy
materials immediately.
Call a Pro: If the smell is strong and persistent, or you see visible mold, get a
mold remediation specialist or a contractor who knows old-house moisture issues.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by catching mold early instead of replacing rotted
wood or major remediation later.

Fix 72 — Keep Stored Items Off Basement Floors and Away
From Walls
The Problem: Stuff piled directly on basement floors or shoved against walls traps
moisture underneath and behind, creating a hidden wet zone that encourages mold
and pests.
Why It Costs Money: Rotting stored items, pest infestations, and mold growth can
all lead to costly cleanups, replacements, and even damage to your home’s framing.
Roger’s First Check: Look around. Are boxes, furniture, or wood stacked on
the bare floor or leaning on the walls? Feel the floor—cold, damp spots
usually mean trouble.
Cheap Fix: Move items onto pallets, shelves, or blocks. Leave a gap
between walls and stored goods for air circulation.
Call a Pro: If you find pests or mold behind stored items, a pest control or
mold specialist might be needed.
Money Saved: $75-$250 for avoiding ruined belongings and pest damage.

Fix 73 — Test a Sump Pump Before the Storm
The Problem: A sump pump that won’t start or can’t handle heavy water inflow
during storms leaves your basement vulnerable to flooding. Old pumps wear out or
get clogged and fail silently.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage repairs after flooding can run into thousands
—flooring, drywall, insulation, electrical fixes—you name it.

## Page 91 (printed page 91)

Roger’s First Check: Pour water into the sump pit and watch if the pump
kicks on and drains properly. Listen for strange noises or sluggish operation.
Cheap Fix: Clean the intake screen and float switch. Replace the pump
battery backup if you have one.
Call a Pro: Call a plumber or pump specialist if the pump doesn’t start, runs
continuously, or you see signs of motor burn-out.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or basement flood cleanup,
potentially $500-$2,500.

Fix 74 — Clean the Sump Pit Without Ignoring the Bigger
Problem
The Problem: Sump pits get filled with dirt, debris, and even small stones, which
can clog the pump and cause failure. But cleaning the pit alone won’t fix water
problems if the surrounding drainage is bad.
Why It Costs Money: Pump failure leads to flooding, and ignoring drainage issues
invites recurring water problems that pile up repair bills.
Roger’s First Check: Scoop out any muck from the sump pit. Then, check
the ground around your house—gutters, downspouts, grading. Is water
draining away from the foundation?
Cheap Fix: Clear gutters and downspouts. Extend downspout discharge at
least 5 feet from the foundation.
Call a Pro: If grading slopes towards your foundation or you have chronic
water pooling, a landscaper or drainage expert can design a fix.
Money Saved: $500-$2,000 by preventing repeated wet basement problems.

Fix 75 — Check Pipe Insulation Before the First Freeze
The Problem: Pipes in basements and crawl spaces are vulnerable to freezing and
bursting when left unprotected in old houses without modern insulation.
Why It Costs Money: A frozen pipe can burst and cause flooding, water damage,
and costly emergency plumbing repairs.

## Page 92 (printed page 92)

Roger’s First Check: Walk your basement or crawl space with a flashlight.
Look for pipes with brittle or missing insulation, especially near exterior walls.
Cheap Fix: Wrap pipes with foam insulation sleeves or fiberglass pipe wrap.
Use heat tape if necessary in very cold spots.
Call a Pro: If you have complex or hidden plumbing needing rerouting or
professional-grade insulation, call a plumber.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or water damage, $500-$2,500.

Fix 76 — Use a Humidity Gauge Before Buying Big
Equipment
The Problem: Basements and crawl spaces have different humidity levels depending on location, ventilation, and soil conditions. Buying a big dehumidifier or
ventilation system without measuring won’t guarantee a fix.
Why It Costs Money: Overbuying equipment wastes money, and underestimating
the problem leads to ongoing moisture damage.
Roger’s First Check: Buy an inexpensive humidity gauge (hygrometer) and
place it in your basement or crawl space for a week. Note the average
humidity level.
Cheap Fix: If humidity is below 60%, improve airflow and use fans first. Only
invest in a dehumidifier if humidity regularly exceeds 60-70%.
Call a Pro: For stubborn humidity problems after basic fixes, a home energy
auditor or HVAC pro can recommend a tailored solution.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by avoiding unnecessary equipment purchases.

Before You Move On: Take a flashlight and your nose to your basement or crawl
space right now. Look around, sniff for dampness, and spot anything stored on the
floor. Check your sump pump if you have one—does it start when you add water? These simple checks cost almost nothing but can save you from serious
headaches. Moisture problems start small, but if you catch them now, you might
avoid repairs that cost thousands down the road. Don’t put off this walk-through
—old houses will tell you what they need if you’re listening.

## Page 94 (printed page 94)

Chapter 14 — Seasonal
Protection for Old Houses
Old houses don’t just sit quiet through the year. They’re like old dogs — they
show their aches and quirks season by season. Spring’s puddles and drips highlight
leaks you might’ve missed all winter. Summer’s heat and humidity can make damp
basements smell worse than last week’s garbage. Fall tells you to tighten up before
winter’s cold snaps turn a forgotten pipe into a busted disaster. Winter punishes
the unprepared with frozen water lines and costly emergency calls.
This chapter covers Fixes 77 through 82, all about timing your attention so your
old house doesn’t turn your wallet inside out. The goal? Catch trouble early, stop
it from growing, and avoid the big-ticket repairs that come from neglecting simple
seasonal chores. It’s not glamorous, but it’s the kind of work that pays off in saved
sweat and dollars.
Roger’s Rule: Half the time spent fixing old houses is watching and listening. The
other half is acting before trouble grows.

Fix 77 — Do the Spring Leak Walkaround
The Problem: After months of snow, ice, and rain, old houses develop leaks in
spots that were dry all winter. Those drips and damp spots can rot wood, ruin
walls, and invite mold.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring leaks leads to damaged framing, ruined finishes,
and mold remediation bills that can run into thousands.
Roger’s First Check: Walk around the whole house with a flashlight. Look
under windows, around chimneys, and where the roof meets the walls.
Check basement ceilings and walls for new damp patches.
Cheap Fix: Reseal cracked caulk or flashing with exterior-grade silicone.
Tighten any loose gutters or downspouts.
Call a Pro: If you find water inside walls or soft spots on framing, get a
carpenter or water-proofing expert.
Money Saved: $150-$600 by stopping small leaks before they rot framing.

## Page 95 (printed page 95)

Fix 78 — Check Exterior Grading Before Blaming the
Basement
The Problem: Water pools near your foundation because the dirt slopes toward the
house instead of away. Old landscaping or settling soil can undo careful grading
work.
Why It Costs Money: Water pooling means wet basements, foundation cracks, and
expensive waterproofing repairs down the road.
Roger’s First Check: After a heavy rain, walk around and see if puddles sit
next to the house. Use a level or even a simple board to check if the soil
slopes away.
Cheap Fix: Add soil and compact it so the ground drops at least 6 inches in
the first 10 feet away from the foundation.
Call a Pro: If you see foundation cracks or the water won’t drain, a landscaper or foundation specialist might be needed.
Money Saved: $500-$2,500 by preventing basement water damage.

Fix 79 — Clean Gutters and Downspouts Before They Mimic
Plumbing Leaks
The Problem: Clogged gutters spill water right against your house, making it look
like a plumbing leak. This water soaks into siding, trim, and the foundation.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage from overflowing gutters leads to wood rot,
siding replacement, and basement leaks.
Roger’s First Check: Get on a ladder or use a gutter scoop to clear out
leaves and debris before heavy spring rains start. Flush the downspouts with
a hose to make sure they’re clear.
Cheap Fix: Install gutter guards or screens to reduce future clogs.
Call a Pro: If gutters are sagging or downspouts disconnected, a gutter
installer or handyman can fix it right.
Money Saved: $200-$1,000 by avoiding water damage repairs.

Fix 80 — Prepare Outdoor Faucets Before the First Freeze
The Problem: Frozen outdoor faucets or hose bibs can burst pipes inside walls or
crawlspaces. Old houses often have uninsulated or poorly insulated plumbing.
Why It Costs Money: Burst pipes mean water damage, drywall repair, and
emergency plumbing bills.

## Page 96 (printed page 96)

Roger’s First Check: Drain and shut off exterior water valves early in fall.
Disconnect hoses. Cover faucets with foam insulators or insulated covers.
Cheap Fix: Wrap exposed pipes with heat tape or foam sleeves.
Call a Pro: If your house doesn’t have shutoff valves for outside water, a
plumber can install them.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call can save $500-$2,000.

Fix 81 — Set Vacation Water Rules Before Leaving Town
The Problem: No matter how careful you are, water leaks happen when you’re
away. Old pipes can fail suddenly, turning your empty house into a swimming
pool.
Why It Costs Money: Water damage while you’re gone can lead to ceiling
collapses, ruined floors, and mold growth.
Roger’s First Check: Shut off the main water valve before you leave, and
drain indoor pipes by opening faucets.
Cheap Fix: Install a water leak detector with automatic shutoff for peace of
mind.
Call a Pro: If you want a smart system that monitors your water remotely, a
plumber or home automation specialist can set it up.
Money Saved: $1,000-$5,000 or more for avoided major water damage.

Fix 82 — Listen for Old-House Winter Warning Sounds
The Problem: Pipes creak, wood shrinks, and heating systems clank in cold
weather. These sounds often warn of stress or failure before you see damage.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring warning noises can lead to frozen pipes bursting or
heating systems failing in the coldest weather.
Roger’s First Check: When it gets cold, listen around your basement,
crawlspace, and near radiators or boilers for new or loud creaks, bangs, or
drips.
Cheap Fix: Tighten loose pipe clamps and add insulation where pipes sound
stressed.
Call a Pro: If you hear water hammer (loud banging in pipes) or suspect pipe
freezing, call a plumber right away.
Money Saved: $150-$1,000 by preventing pipe bursts or heating failure.

## Page 97 (printed page 97)

Before you move on, grab a calendar or planner and mark out these seasonal tasks.
Set reminders to do your leak walkaround in spring and gutter cleaning before the
rains hit. Prepare outdoor faucets and shut off valves in fall. That calendar is like a
small investment in peace of mind — it helps you avoid those emergency calls
that cost way more than a few hours of regular maintenance. Old houses demand
attention, but a little seasonal care keeps them solid for years.

## Page 101 (printed page 101)

Chapter 15 — Maintenance Habits
That Pay You Back
I’ve been in old houses long enough to know the cheapest repair is the one you
never have to make. Fixing a big leak, replacing a rotted sill, or chasing down
water damage after a burst pipe will cost you a lot more than a little regular
upkeep. This chapter covers Fixes 83 through 91 — simple maintenance habits
that turn your old-house headaches into manageable, even routine, tasks.
It’s easy to let things slide in an old house. You think, “I’ll check that valve or
fixture later.” Then later turns into a leak that ruins your hardwood floors or a
frozen pipe that bursts in the middle of winter. But what if a few minutes every
month or quarter could catch problems early? What if you had a small parts bin
ready and a plan for checking your house twice a year? That’s what this chapter
offers: cheap prevention that beats expensive repairs.
Some of these fixes involve a flashlight and a quick look under your sinks or
around your water heater. Others are about developing habits, like running unused
fixtures or testing shutoff valves. These aren’t glamorous tasks, but they pay off in
fewer emergencies and lower repair bills.
You don’t have to turn your life upside down either. I like to schedule two old-house maintenance weekends each year and spend about 30 minutes quarterly on a
quick checkup — a habit that’s saved me and my customers thousands over the
years. The key is consistency and knowing what to look for.
Roger’s Rule: A stitch in time saves more than nine — it saves your floors,
walls, and wallet.

Fix 83 — Do a Five-Minute Monthly Leak Check
The Problem: Tiny leaks often go unnoticed until they cause water damage or
mold. Old plumbing joints and old galvanized pipes are especially prone to slow
drips.
Why It Costs Money: A steady drip can waste hundreds of gallons and cause rot
or mold behind walls, leading to costly repairs. Plus, your water bill balloons for
no good reason.

## Page 102 (printed page 102)

Roger’s First Check: Shine a flashlight under sinks, around water heaters,
and near exposed pipes. Look for wet spots, mineral deposits, or corrosion.
Cheap Fix: Tighten connections with a wrench or replace a worn washer—
both cost under $10 and minutes of your time.
Call a Pro: If the leak comes from within a wall or a stubborn valve, call a
plumber before it worsens.
Money Saved: $75-$250 in water and minor damage repairs.

Fix 84 — Run Unused Fixtures to Keep Traps Wet
The Problem: In homes with multiple bathrooms or seasonal use, traps dry out and
let sewer gas into your living space.
Why It Costs Money: Dry traps can cause health hazards, and the smell alone
might drive you to expensive fixes or replacements.
Roger’s First Check: Turn on every sink, tub, and floor drain at least once a
month, running water long enough to refill the trap.
Cheap Fix: Simply run water for a minute—no parts needed.
Call a Pro: If you smell sewage despite regular use, a plumber can inspect
venting and trap seals.
Money Saved: One avoided call for odor investigation or trap replacement,
usually $150-$600.

Fix 85 — Clean Aerators and Showerheads Before Replacing
Fixtures
The Problem: Mineral buildup in aerators and showerheads reduces water flow and
pressure, making you think it’s time for a costly fixture replacement.
Why It Costs Money: Buying new fixtures isn’t cheap. Sometimes you just need
to clean the parts.
Roger’s First Check: Unscrew aerators and soak them in vinegar for an
hour to dissolve mineral deposits.
Cheap Fix: Cleaning aerators and showerheads restores flow and saves a
fixture purchase.
Call a Pro: If the flow is still weak after cleaning, a plumber can check for
bigger issues like clogged pipes.
Money Saved: $50-$150 per fixture.

## Page 103 (printed page 103)

Fix 86 — Test Shutoff Valves Twice a Year
The Problem: Shutoff valves in old houses often seize up from lack of use or
corrosion. When you need them, they won’t budge.
Why It Costs Money: Emergency repairs get pricier when you can’t shut off water
quickly. Burst pipes or leaks can flood and damage your home.
Roger’s First Check: Turn every shutoff valve slowly in both directions to
keep them operable.
Cheap Fix: Apply penetrating oil to stuck valves and exercise them regularly.
Call a Pro: If a valve leaks or won’t turn, replace it before an emergency happens.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or flood repair, $500-$2,500.

Fix 87 — Replace Small Rubber Parts Before They Waste Big
Money
The Problem: Rubber washers, gaskets, and seals in your plumbing wear out and
harden over time, leading to slow leaks or sudden failures.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring these small parts can cause bigger leaks, pipe
damage, and water waste.
Roger’s First Check: Inspect faucet washers and hose bib seals every six
months for cracks or stiffness.
Cheap Fix: Keep a supply of washers and seals on hand and swap them out
at the first sign of wear.
Call a Pro: For internal valve seals or complicated faucet repairs, call a
plumber.
Money Saved: $75-$250 per repair avoided.

Fix 88 — Use Water Alarms in the Right Places
The Problem: Water leaks sometimes happen behind walls or under appliances
where you can’t see damage until it’s severe.
Why It Costs Money: Unseen leaks ruin floors, walls, and ceilings, and the repairs
can be brutal.

## Page 104 (printed page 104)

Roger’s First Check: Place battery-operated water alarms near water heaters, sump pumps, dishwashers, and under sinks.
Cheap Fix: Water alarms cost $15-$30 and alert you early, letting you catch
leaks before damage spreads.
Call a Pro: When the alarm sounds, track down the leak or call a plumber
immediately.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency repair, $500-$2,000.

Fix 89 — Keep a Parts Bin for Repeat Old-House Problems
The Problem: Old houses often have quirky plumbing parts that aren’t available at
your local big-box store. Running out means delays and emergency trips.
Why It Costs Money: Waiting for parts or paying rush fees leads to bigger
problems and higher repair bills.
Roger’s First Check: Keep common parts like washers, packing rings,
faucet stems, and shutoff valves on hand.
Cheap Fix: Spend a little now on parts from specialty suppliers and avoid
costly emergencies later.
Call a Pro: When a unique part needs replacement and you don’t have it, a
plumber can source and install it quickly.
Money Saved: $75-$250 per avoided emergency trip.

Fix 90 — Set Two Old-House Maintenance Weekends Per
Year
The Problem: Without dedicated time, maintenance tasks get pushed aside indefinitely.
Why It Costs Money: Neglected maintenance leads to costly surprises and
emergency repairs.

## Page 105 (printed page 105)

Roger’s First Check: Block two weekends a year on your calendar for old-house upkeep tasks.
Cheap Fix: Use these weekends to run your quarterly 30-minute check,
clean fixtures, test valves, and restock your parts bin.
Call a Pro: Schedule any repairs or inspections you can’t do yourself during
or after these weekends.
Money Saved: Hundreds to thousands by preventing emergencies and
extending your home’s life.

Fix 91 — Make the 100-Fix Checklist a House Project Plan
The Problem: Without a clear plan, maintenance can feel random and overwhelming.
Why It Costs Money: Tasks get forgotten or neglected, leading to bigger repairs.
Roger’s First Check: Organize the fixes into a checklist or calendar,
breaking them into manageable chunks.
Cheap Fix: Use a simple notebook, spreadsheet, or app to track what’s done
and what’s next.
Call a Pro: Share your plan with your plumber or handyman to schedule
professional help efficiently.
Money Saved: Avoided emergency costs and better budgeting, $150-$600
or more.

Before You Move On
Don’t wait for a crisis to start these habits. Grab a flashlight and spend five
minutes under your sinks this week. Check for leaks, run any unused taps, and
take note of what needs attention. If you don’t have a shutoff valve that works,
plan to fix that before winter. Keep a small bin of washers and seals handy. And
mark two weekends on your calendar for a proper house checkup — I promise,
it’s time well spent. These simple habits keep your old house running smoother
and your repair bills smaller. Little efforts now can save you big headaches later.

## Page 107 (printed page 107)

Chapter 16 — Spending Smarter
When You Do Need Help
Fixes 92 through 100 bring us into the part of old-house ownership that’s not just
about rolling up your sleeves but knowing when and how to bring in a pro without
throwing your hard-earned cash out the window. You can save thousands not just
by doing things yourself, but by spending smarter when you do have to call in
help. It sounds simple, but most folks don’t realize that a little prep goes a long
way toward avoiding confusion, unnecessary repairs, and overpriced emergency
calls.
Older houses come with quirks. That means contractors will often need extra time
figuring out what’s going on—unless you’re ready with photos, clear questions,
and a sense of what’s urgent and what’s not. You don’t want to be the customer
who says, “Fix it,” then gets stuck with a bill for replacing parts that could have
been repaired. A little homework on your end can save you from paying for
“surprises” or second visits.
I want you to think of this chapter as your checklist for when it’s time to bring in
a pro. Knowing the difference between a quick fix and a full replacement, how to
ask the right questions, and how to prepare your home’s paperwork will make
those calls less stressful and more wallet-friendly. The Contractor Call Preparation
Sheet I mention later is a tool I’ve seen work wonders for homeowners who want
to keep their repair costs in check.
Roger’s Rule:
If you don’t understand the work, don’t approve the bill. Get clear answers, take
photos, and avoid the “just fix it” trap.

Fix 92 — Know When a Service Call Is Actually the Cheap
Option
The Problem: Trying to DIY every little plumbing or electrical issue can backfire.
Sometimes what looks like a simple fix turns into a costly mess if you’re not sure
what you’re doing.

## Page 108 (printed page 108)

Why It Costs Money: Wasting time and materials on a failed DIY job means
paying twice—once for your mistakes, once for the pro to clean up. Plus, some
problems can worsen if ignored or handled improperly.
Roger’s First Check: Is this repair outside your comfort zone or skill set?
Are you facing a leak from a hidden pipe or a wiring issue with old knob-and-tube?
Cheap Fix: Try tightening a loose valve or resetting a breaker if you know
how. Otherwise, call a pro for an assessment before tearing things apart.
Call a Pro: When you spot signs like persistent leaks, burnt smells, or
sparks, don’t wait. Paying for a qualified technician’s service call early can
save thousands in water damage or fire risk.
Money Saved: One avoided emergency call or flood cleanup can save
$500–$2,500 or more.

Fix 93 — Ask Better Questions Before Approving a Repair
The Problem: Contractors often throw jargon or vague explanations at you, hoping
you’ll nod and sign the work order.
Why It Costs Money: Without clear answers, you might pay for unnecessary replacements or upgrades. Plus, unclear scope can mean surprise fees.
Roger’s First Check: Ask, “Can you show me the problem? What exactly
needs fixing? Are there cheaper alternatives?”
Cheap Fix: Prepare a list of questions before the pro arrives. If they can’t
explain the issue and solution plainly, that’s a red flag.
Call a Pro: If the contractor is patient, transparent, and willing to educate,
you’re in good hands. Otherwise, get a second opinion.
Money Saved: Avoided upsells or unnecessary part swaps can save $150–
$600.

Fix 94 — Get the Right Photos Before the Contractor Arrives
The Problem: When you call a pro without pictures, they often schedule appointments just to diagnose. That doubles the labor cost.
Why It Costs Money: Extra visits mean extra charges. Plus, you lose time waiting
for repairs.

## Page 109 (printed page 109)

Roger’s First Check: Use your phone to snap clear photos of the problem
area, including any labels, model numbers, or damage.
Cheap Fix: Send these photos ahead to the contractor. It helps them prepare
parts and tools before they get there.
Call a Pro: If you can’t safely access the area or the problem is hidden, get
the pro out sooner rather than later. But photos always help.
Money Saved: One fewer visit can save $75–$250.

Fix 95 — Separate Emergency Pricing From Real Urgency
The Problem: Contractors often charge premium rates for “emergency” calls, but
not every problem is an emergency.
Why It Costs Money: Paying emergency fees for non-urgent repairs adds hundreds
of dollars to your bill unnecessarily.
Roger’s First Check: Does the issue pose immediate danger—like a gas
leak, flooding, or electrical sparking—or is it a nuisance that can wait a day or
two?
Cheap Fix: Schedule non-emergency repairs during regular hours. Keep an
eye on leaks and electrical issues but don’t panic over a slow drip.
Call a Pro: Call emergency services only when safety is at stake. Otherwise,
book regular appointments.
Money Saved: Skipping emergency fees can save $200–$500 per call.

Fix 96 — Avoid Replacing What Can Be Repaired
The Problem: Old-house contractors sometimes recommend replacing parts because
they’re unfamiliar with repairing vintage fixtures or materials.
Why It Costs Money: Replacement often costs way more than a skilled repair or
part refurbishment.

## Page 110 (printed page 110)

Roger’s First Check: Ask if the part can be fixed or patched first. Old cast-iron pipes, brass valves, and woodwork often can be saved.
Cheap Fix: Find a pro with old-house experience or look for specialty repair
shops.
Call a Pro: When the pro offers repair options, weigh them before saying yes
to full replacement.
Money Saved: A good repair vs. replacement can save $150–$800, or more
on plumbing and woodwork.

Fix 97 — Know When Replacement Beats Another Patch
The Problem: Sometimes you patch a problem only to have it reappear because the
underlying issue is worse than it looks.
Why It Costs Money: Multiple patches add up, and repeated visits cost more than
a proper replacement.
Roger’s First Check: Look for signs of widespread damage—rotted wood,
corroded pipes, or cracked foundation—that won’t hold up after another
patch.
Cheap Fix: If the patch is holding and the problem is minor, wait and watch.
But budget for replacement when damage spreads.
Call a Pro: When repairs fail repeatedly, invest in replacement to avoid
endless calls.
Money Saved: Avoiding repeated calls and patch jobs can save $500–
$2,000 over time.

Fix 98 — Keep Receipts, Model Numbers, and Part Sizes in
One Place
The Problem: Digging through a pile of receipts or searching for model numbers
during an emergency wastes time and can lead to ordering wrong parts.
Why It Costs Money: Wrong parts mean returns, delays, and extra labor costs.
Plus, you might pay more for rush orders.

## Page 111 (printed page 111)

Roger’s First Check: Create a dedicated binder or digital folder with all your
receipts, warranty info, and part details.
Cheap Fix: Update it every time you buy or replace something in your house.
Take photos of labels and stickers on appliances and fixtures.
Call a Pro: When you provide accurate info upfront, contractors can bring the
right parts and fix things faster.
Money Saved: Prevented delays and wrong-parts orders can save $75–
$300.

Fix 99 — Use Home Inspection Reports as a Repair Roadmap
The Problem: Many old-house owners get an inspection report once and then
ignore it until something breaks.
Why It Costs Money: Ignoring the report means you miss chances to plan repairs
and budget for replacements before emergencies strike.
Roger’s First Check: Review your inspection report yearly. Highlight items
needing attention soon and those to watch for.
Cheap Fix: Prioritize repairs by urgency and budget. Don’t let small issues
grow into disasters.
Call a Pro: Share your inspection report with contractors. It speeds diagnosis
and helps them plan.
Money Saved: Planned repairs often cost less than emergency fixes, saving
hundreds to thousands.

Fix 100 — Do It Once, Do It Right: Roger’s Final Rule for Old-House Owners
The Problem: Cutting corners or rushing repairs on an old house leads to repeat
visits, bigger damage, and frustration.
Why It Costs Money: Skimping on quality parts, workmanship, or prep causes you
to pay twice or thrice over time.

## Page 112 (printed page 112)

Roger’s First Check: Evaluate whether you’re tackling the repair with the
right tools, skills, and materials.
Cheap Fix: Invest in quality parts and hire pros who know old houses when
needed. It’s worth the upfront cost.
Call a Pro: When in doubt, get a trusted contractor with old-house
experience to do it right the first time.
Money Saved: Avoiding repeat repairs can save $500–$2,500 or more over
the life of your home.

Before You Move On
You’ve got a toolbox full of ways to save when calling in help. Now, take a few
minutes to gather those photos, jot down the questions you want to ask your next
contractor, and pull together your receipts and inspection reports. Think about what
really counts as an emergency and what can wait. This little prep work might not
feel like fixing a leak or patching plaster, but it’s the kind of smart move that
keeps your house running and your bank account from running dry. When you’re
ready to pick up the phone, you’ll be spending smarter, not just hoping for the
best.

Seasonal Old-House Maintenance Calendar
Old houses change with the weather. Use this calendar to make prevention automatic.

| Season or Timing | What to Check |
|---|---|
| Every month | Look under sinks, around toilets, near the water heater, at the sump area, and around visible basement pipes. |
| Every quarter | Test water alarms, run unused fixtures, clean aerators, inspect supply lines, and update the repair log. |
| Spring | Walk the exterior after winter, check hose bibbs, basement corners, downspouts, grading, and ceiling stains after rain. |
| Summer | Watch humidity, musty smells, slow drains, disposal odors, and condensation around cold pipes. |
| Fall | Disconnect hoses, find indoor hose-bibb shutoffs, inspect pipe insulation, test sump pump, and clear gutters. |
| Winter | Listen for new pipe noises, watch pressure changes, keep vulnerable areas warm, and investigate any sudden dripping or running-water sound. |
| Once a year | Review water-heater age, repair receipts, shutoff labels, contractor notes, and the 100-fix checklist. |

## Page 121 (printed page 121)

Symptom-to-First-Check Troubleshooting Guide
When something looks wrong, start with the simplest safe check. If water is active,
sewage is involved, electrical hazards are nearby, or you do not know how to
isolate the problem, stop and get help.

| Symptom | First Check | Call a Pro When |
|---|---|---|
| Ceiling stain | Check whether it changes after rain, shower use, toilet use, or HVAC operation. | Stop using nearby fixtures if active water appears. |
| Drip under sink | Dry everything and use the paper-towel test at supply lines, drain body, trap, and shutoff. | If the valve or wall pipe is corroded or moving. |
| Sewer smell | Run water in unused fixtures to refill traps. | If multiple fixtures smell, gurgle, or back up. |
| Slow bathroom sink | Remove and clean the stopper before using tools deeper in the drain. | If several drains slow at once. |
| Weak toilet flush | Check tank water level, chain slack, flapper, and rim holes. | If the toilet rocks, leaks at the base, or backs up. |
| Running toilet | Dye-test the tank and inspect flapper, chain, and fill valve. | If shutoff valve leaks or will not move. |
| Low faucet flow | Clean aerator before blaming whole-house pressure. | If flow dropped suddenly throughout the house. |
| Basement dampness | Check humidity, stored items, wall stains, sump pit, exterior grade, and downspouts. | If water enters repeatedly or mold is visible. |
| Outdoor faucet drip | Remove hose, check packing nut and indoor shutoff location. | If water appears inside wall or basement after use. |
| No hot water | Check water-heater age, power/gas status, leaks, and error lights without bypassing safety devices. | For gas, electrical, tank leaks, or T&P discharge. |

control active damage if safe, then gather details.

Tools and Cheap Parts List
Do not buy a truck full of tools. Build a practical old-house first-aid shelf and add
to it as your house teaches you what repeats.

| Category | Useful Items |
|---|---|
| Safety | Gloves, eye protection, flashlight/headlamp, dust mask, knee pad, bucket, towels, drop cloth. |
| Leak control | Pipe repair clamp, plumber’s tape, adjustable wrench, tongue-and-groove pliers, utility knife, water alarms. |
| Sink and faucet basics | Aerator key, replacement aerators, O-rings, washers, basin wrench, small brush, white vinegar. |
| Toilet basics | Universal flapper, fill valve kit, supply line, wax ring only when reseating is appropriate, toilet shims. |
| Drain basics | Cup plunger, flange plunger, hand snake, plastic hair tool, trap brush, bucket. |
| Documentation | Repair log, permanent marker, valve labels, tape measure, phone photo album folder. |
| Seasonal | Hose washers, hose caps, pipe insulation, outdoor faucet cover, humidity gauge. |

## Page 123 (printed page 123)

| Glossary Term | Plain-English Meaning |
|---|---|
| Anode rod | A sacrificial metal rod inside many tank water heaters that helps protect the tank from corrosion. |
| Cleanout | An access point in a drain line used by professionals to clear or inspect the pipe. |
| Compression fitting | A fitting that seals by squeezing a ring or ferrule around tubing as the nut tightens. |
| Flapper | The rubber part in a toilet tank that lifts during a flush and seals water in the tank afterward. |
| Fill valve | The toilet tank part that refills the tank after a flush. |
| Galvanized pipe | Older steel pipe coated with zinc that can rust, clog internally, and reduce flow over time. |
| Hose bibb | An outdoor faucet connection, usually where a garden hose attaches. |
| P-trap | The curved drain fitting under a sink or fixture that holds water to block sewer gas. |
| Packing nut | A nut around a valve stem that can sometimes be gently tightened to stop a stem leak. |
| Shutoff valve | A valve that stops water to a fixture, appliance, branch line, or the whole house. |
| Supply line | A pressurized tube or pipe that brings clean water to a faucet, toilet, or appliance. |
| T&P valve | The temperature-and-pressure relief valve on a water heater, a critical safety device. |
| Vent stack | A plumbing vent that helps drains flow and sewer gases leave safely through the roof. |
| Wax ring | The seal between a toilet and the drain flange beneath it. |

## Page 124 (printed page 124)

Resources
Use manufacturer manuals for fixture-specific parts, local building departments for
permit questions, utility companies for gas and water emergency procedures, and
licensed professionals for work involving hazards. For older homes, also consider
qualified environmental testing when lead, asbestos, mold, or contaminated water
may be involved.
Keep model numbers, installation dates, service stickers, and repair receipts in one
place. The best resource for your old house is the record you build while paying
attention.

About Roger
Roger the Pipe Guy is a 45-year plumber and plainspoken homeowner advocate
who has spent a lifetime seeing how small problems turn into big bills. His advice
is built around a simple idea: before you spend a dime, know what you are
looking at.
Roger’s goal is not to turn every homeowner into a contractor. It is to help old-house owners recognize the clues, stop avoidable damage, ask better questions, and
know when a cheap fix is smart — and when stopping is the smartest fix of all.
Roger’s Final Rule: Do it once, do it right, and do not let the house bully
you.
